**Women's suffrage** is the [right of women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_rights "Women's rights") to [vote in elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffrage "Suffrage"). Historically, women rarely had the right to vote, even in ostensibly democratic systems of government.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-:2-1) The 19th century saw many movements advocating "universal [male] suffrage", most notably in Europe and North America; following this, movements for women's suffrage became prominent, and between the late 19th century and the early 20th century, women's suffrage was accomplished in Australasia, then Europe, and then the Americas.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-3)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-:2-1)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-4) By the middle of the 20th century, women's suffrage had been established as a [norm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_norm "Social norm") of democratic governance.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-:2-1) Extended political campaigns by women and their male supporters played a central role in changing public attitudes, altering norms, and achieving legislation or constitutional amendments for women's suffrage.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-:2-1)

The first wave of women's suffrage took place in 1893–1930, covering English-speaking countries, Scandinavian states, and some other parts of Europe.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-:2-1) The experience of the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") has been characterized as an important factor in shifting public support for women's suffrage.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-5) The second wave, 1930–1970, covered nearly all Latin-American countries, much of Sub-Saharan Africa and some European laggards (France, Spain, Belgium).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-:2-1)

Prior to 1893, there were instances where women could vote in some elections and at the subnational level. The first national granting of women's suffrage was in 1893 in the then self-governing[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-6) British [colony of New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colony_of_New_Zealand "Colony of New Zealand"). National and international organizations formed to coordinate efforts towards women voting, especially the [International Woman Suffrage Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Alliance_of_Women "International Alliance of Women") (founded in 1904 in [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin"), Germany).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-7) Most major Western powers extended voting rights to women by the interwar period, including Canada (1917), Germany (1918), [Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria "Austria"), the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands") (1919), the United States (1920) and the United Kingdom (1928).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-8) Notable exceptions in Europe were France, where women could not vote until 1944, [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece "Greece") (equal voting rights for women did not exist there until 1952, although, since 1930, literate women were able to vote in local elections), and [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland "Switzerland") (where, since 1971, women could vote at the federal level, and between 1959 and 1990, women got the right to vote at the local canton level).

In many countries, limited suffrage for women was granted before [universal suffrage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_suffrage "Universal suffrage") for men; for instance, literate women or property owners were granted suffrage before all men received it. The United Nations encouraged women's suffrage in the years following World War II, and the [Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convention_on_the_Elimination_of_All_Forms_of_Discrimination_Against_Women "Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women") (1979) identifies it as a basic right with 189 countries currently being parties to this convention.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Women%27s_suffrage&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

For a chronological guide, see [Timeline of women's suffrage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_women's_suffrage "Timeline of women's suffrage").

[![Image 10](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c9/AnnaIIStolQued.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:AnnaIIStolQued.jpg)

[Anna II, Abbess of Quedlinburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_II,_Abbess_of_Quedlinburg "Anna II, Abbess of Quedlinburg"). In the pre-modern era in some parts of Europe, [abbesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbess "Abbess") were permitted to participate and vote in various European national assemblies by virtue of their rank within the Roman Catholic and Protestant churches.

### Before the 19th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Women%27s_suffrage&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Before the 19th century")]

In ancient [Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athenian_democracy "Athenian democracy"), often cited as the birthplace of democracy, only adult male citizens could vote. Women, slaves, and [metics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metic "Metic") (resident foreigners) could not.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Through subsequent centuries, Europe was ruled by monarchs, though various forms of parliament arose at different times. The high rank ascribed to [abbesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbess "Abbess") within the [Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") permitted some women the right to sit and vote at national assemblies – as with various high-ranking abbesses in Medieval Germany, who were ranked among the independent princes of the empire. Their Protestant successors enjoyed the same privilege almost into modern times.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-Abbess-9)

[Marie Guyart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Guyart "Marie Guyart"), a French nun who worked with the [First Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Nations_in_Canada "First Nations in Canada") people of Canada during the 17th century, wrote in 1654 regarding the suffrage practices of [Iroquois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iroquois "Iroquois") women: "These female chieftains... have a deciding vote in the councils. They make decisions there like their male counterparts, and it is they who even delegated as first ambassadors to discuss peace."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-10) The Iroquois, like many First Nations in North America,[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] had a [matrilineal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrilineal "Matrilineal")[kinship system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinship_system "Kinship system"). Property and descent were passed through the female line. Women elders voted on hereditary male chiefs and could depose them.

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/74/Catherine_Helen_Spence.jpg/250px-Catherine_Helen_Spence.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Catherine_Helen_Spence.jpg)

[South Australian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Australia "South Australia") suffragist [Catherine Helen Spence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_Helen_Spence "Catherine Helen Spence") stood for office in 1897. In a first for the modern world, South Australia granted women the right to stand for Parliament in 1895.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-SA1895-11)

[![Image 12](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/75/Marie_Stritt.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Marie_Stritt.jpg)

[Marie Stritt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Stritt "Marie Stritt") (1855–1928), German suffragist, co-founder of the [International Alliance of Women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Alliance_of_Women "International Alliance of Women")

The first independent country to introduce women's suffrage was arguably Sweden. In Sweden, conditional women's suffrage was in effect during the [Age of Liberty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Liberty "Age of Liberty") (1718–1772).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-Karlsson_Sj%C3%B6gren-12)

In 1756, [Lydia Taft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydia_Taft "Lydia Taft") became the first legal woman voter in colonial America. This occurred under [British rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_North_America "British North America") in the [Massachusetts Colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Massachusetts_Bay "Province of Massachusetts Bay").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-address-13) In a [New England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England "New England")[town meeting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_meeting "Town meeting") in [Uxbridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uxbridge,_Massachusetts "Uxbridge, Massachusetts"), Massachusetts, she voted on at least three occasions.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-blacks-14)

Under the July 2, 1776 declaration of its independence from English rule, unmarried white women who owned property could vote in [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey "New Jersey") and that remained unchanged until 1807.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-15)

In the 1792 elections in [Sierra Leone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Leone "Sierra Leone"), then a new British colony, all heads of household could vote and one-third were ethnic African women.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-16)

Before the 19th century, some countries granted women the right to vote partially or temporarily:[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-17)

*   in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome"), in 1591, during the short pontificate of Pope [Innocent IX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Innocent_IX "Innocent IX") (November–December 1591), men and women over 14 years old had the right to vote;
*   in [Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden "Sweden"), between 1718 and 1771, major single or widowed women (married women are excluded), owners, subject to tax and members of guilds were authorized to participate in local and national elections. These rights were annulled in 1758 for local elections and in 1772 for national elections. The right to vote in municipal elections was again granted to major single women, taxable and owners between 1862 and 1919;
*   the [Republic of Corsica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Corsica "Republic of Corsica") in 1755, and until its fall in 1769, implicitly granted the right to vote to single or widowed women (the electoral majority being set at 25 years);
*   in [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), under the [Ancien Régime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancien_R%C3%A9gime "Ancien Régime"), women legally declared heads of family (widows, single women, or in cases of the husband's absence) had the right to vote in municipal assemblies until 1789. From 1302 until 1789, noble women who owned fiefs and mother abbesses were summoned to the [Estates General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estates_General_(France) "Estates General (France)") to elect their representatives. In the elections to the Estates General of 1789, members of religious communities were admitted to vote, as well as, for the [Third Estate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Estate "Third Estate"), heads of agricultural or business operations, and in the cities, members of trade bodies and communities. Women were then explicitly excluded from the electorate starting from the elections to the [Legislative Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legislative_Assembly_(France) "Legislative Assembly (France)") of 1791 and until 1945.

Territorial entities, subnational, non-state or not recognized, also preceded many countries:[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-18)

*   the State of [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey "New Jersey") ([United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States")) from 1776 to 1807 under the condition, as for men, of being themselves owners;
*   [Lower Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Canada "Lower Canada") (British colonial province corresponding partially to current [Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec "Quebec") and [Labrador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labrador "Labrador")), from 1791 and under the condition, as for men, of being themselves owners, restricted in 1834 and finally withdrawn after the [Rebellions of 1837–1838](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebellions_of_1837%E2%80%931838 "Rebellions of 1837–1838"), in 1849;
*   the [Pitcairn Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitcairn_Islands "Pitcairn Islands") ([United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") dependency) in 1838;
*   the Mormon State of [Deseret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_Deseret "State of Deseret") (1847) (became [Utah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah "Utah") in 1850);
*   the province of [Vélez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%A9lez_Province "Vélez Province") ([Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia "Colombia")) from 1853 to its integration into the federal State of Santander in 1857;
*   the territory of [Wyoming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyoming "Wyoming") (United States) in 1869 with right to eligibility. A few months later in 1870, a woman was elected justice of the peace in [Laramie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laramie,_Wyoming "Laramie, Wyoming"), the same year in the same city another is elected court bailiff (Court Bailiff);
*   the territory of [Utah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah "Utah") (United States) in 1870. A federal Congressional act suppressed it in 1887;
*   the [Isle of Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Man "Isle of Man") (United Kingdom dependency) in 1881;
*   the territory of [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Territory "Washington Territory") in 1883, suppressed by the [Supreme Court of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") in 1887;
*   Wyoming as a state in 1890;
*   [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado "Colorado") (United States) in 1893;
*   the [Cook Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook_Islands "Cook Islands") (British protectorate) in 1893;
*   [South Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Australia "South Australia") (autonomous British colony) from 1895; became one of the first territories in the world to allow women to be candidates in legislative elections;
*   Utah (admission to the Union) and [Idaho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idaho "Idaho") (United States) in 1896.

Other early instances of women's suffrage included the [Corsican Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corsican_Republic "Corsican Republic") (1755), the Pitcairn Islands (1838), the Isle of Man (1881), and [Franceville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franceville,_New_Hebrides "Franceville, New Hebrides") (1889–1890); but some of these operated only briefly as independent states, and others were not clearly independent.

South Australian suffragist [Catherine Helen Spence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_Helen_Spence "Catherine Helen Spence") stood for office in 1897. In a first for the modern world, South Australia granted women the right to stand for Parliament in 1895.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-19)

### 19th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Women%27s_suffrage&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 19th century")]

The female descendants of the [_Bounty_ mutineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutiny_on_the_Bounty "Mutiny on the Bounty") who lived on [Pitcairn Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitcairn_Islands "Pitcairn Islands") could vote from 1838. This right was transferred after they resettled in 1856 to [Norfolk Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norfolk_Island "Norfolk Island") (now an Australian external territory).[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-elections.org.nz-20)

The emergence of modern democracy generally began with male citizens obtaining the right to vote in advance of female citizens, except in the [Kingdom of Hawai'i](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hawai'i "Kingdom of Hawai'i"), where universal suffrage was introduced in 1840 without mention of sex; however, a constitutional amendment in 1852 rescinded female voting and put property qualifications on male voting.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-Kauanui_2018_187%E2%80%93189-21)

The seed for the first Woman's Rights Convention in the United States in [Seneca Falls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seneca_Falls_Convention "Seneca Falls Convention"), New York, was planted in 1840, when [Elizabeth Cady Stanton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Cady_Stanton "Elizabeth Cady Stanton") met [Lucretia Mott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucretia_Mott "Lucretia Mott") at the [World Anti-Slavery Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Anti-Slavery_Convention "World Anti-Slavery Convention") in London. The conference refused to seat Mott and other women delegates from the U.S. because of their sex. In 1851, Stanton met temperance worker [Susan B. Anthony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_B._Anthony "Susan B. Anthony"), and shortly the two would be joined in the long struggle to secure the vote for women in the U.S. In 1868 Anthony encouraged working women from the printing and sewing trades in New York, who were excluded from men's trade unions, to form Working Women's Associations. As a delegate to the National Labor Congress in 1868, Anthony persuaded the committee on female labor to call for votes for women and equal pay for equal work. The men at the conference deleted the reference to the vote.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-22) In the US, women in the [Wyoming Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyoming_Territory "Wyoming Territory") were permitted to both vote and stand for office in 1869.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-Wyoming-23) Subsequent American suffrage groups often disagreed on tactics, with the [National American Woman Suffrage Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_American_Woman_Suffrage_Association "National American Woman Suffrage Association") arguing for a state-by-state campaign and the [National Woman's Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Woman's_Party "National Woman's Party") focusing on an amendment to the U.S. Constitution.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-26)

The [1840 constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1840_Constitution_of_the_Hawaiian_Kingdom "1840 Constitution of the Hawaiian Kingdom") of the Kingdom of Hawaii established a House of Representatives, but did not specify who was eligible to participate in the election of it. Some academics have argued that this omission enabled women to vote in the first elections, in which votes were cast by means of signatures on [petitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petition "Petition"); but this interpretation remains controversial.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-27) The [second constitution of 1852](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1852_Constitution_of_the_Hawaiian_Kingdom "1852 Constitution of the Hawaiian Kingdom") specified that suffrage was restricted to males over twenty years-old.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-Kauanui_2018_187%E2%80%93189-21)

In 1849, the [Grand Duchy of Tuscany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Duchy_of_Tuscany "Grand Duchy of Tuscany"), in Italy, was the first European state to have a law that provided for the vote of women, for administrative elections, taking up a tradition that was already informally sometimes present in Italy.

The 1853 Constitution of the province of [Vélez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%A9lez_Province "Vélez Province") in the [Republic of New Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_New_Granada "Republic of New Granada"), modern day [Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia "Colombia"), allowed for married women, or women older than the age of 21, the right to vote within the province. However, this law was subsequently annulled by the [Supreme Court of the Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Justice_of_Colombia "Supreme Court of Justice of Colombia"), arguing that the citizens of the province could not have more rights than those already guaranteed to the citizens of the other provinces of the country, thus eliminating female suffrage from this province in 1856.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-30)

In 1881, the [Isle of Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Man "Isle of Man"), an internally self-governing dependent territory of the British Crown, enfranchised women property owners. With this it provided the first action for women's suffrage within the [British Isles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Isles "British Isles").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-elections.org.nz-20)

The [Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean") commune of [Franceville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franceville,_New_Hebrides "Franceville, New Hebrides") (now [Port Vila, Vanuatu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Vila,_Vanuatu "Port Vila, Vanuatu")), maintained independence from 1889 to 1890, becoming the first [self-governing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-governance "Self-governance") nation to adopt universal suffrage without distinction of sex or color, although only white males were permitted to hold office.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-31)

For countries that have their origins in self-governing colonies but later became independent nations in the 20th century, the [Colony of New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colony_of_New_Zealand "Colony of New Zealand") was the first to acknowledge women's right to vote in 1893, largely due to a movement led by [Kate Sheppard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kate_Sheppard "Kate Sheppard"). The British protectorate of [Cook Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook_Islands "Cook Islands") rendered the same right in 1893 as well.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-32) Another British colony, [South Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Australia "South Australia"), followed in 1895, [enacting laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_Amendment_(Adult_Suffrage)_Act_1894 "Constitutional Amendment (Adult Suffrage) Act 1894") which not only extended voting to women, but also made women eligible to stand for election to its parliament.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-:0-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-FennaRobbins2013-34)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-36)

### 20th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Women%27s_suffrage&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 20th century")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/French_pro_women%27s_suffrage_poster_1934.jpg/250px-French_pro_women%27s_suffrage_poster_1934.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:French_pro_women's_suffrage_poster_1934.jpg)

French pro-suffrage poster, 1934, whose message begins: "In all the great countries of Europe, women vote or want to vote; French women do not vote! French women want to vote!"

Following the [federation of the British colonies in Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Australia "Federation of Australia") in 1901, the new federal government enacted the [Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Franchise_Act_1902 "Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902") which allowed female [British subjects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_subject "British subject") to vote and stand for election on the same terms as men. However, many [indigenous Australians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_Australians "Indigenous Australians") remained excluded from voting federally until 1962.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-Indigenous_Australians-37)

The first place in Europe to introduce women's suffrage was the [Grand Duchy of Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Duchy_of_Finland "Grand Duchy of Finland") in 1906, and it also became the first place in continental Europe to implement racially-equal suffrage for women.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-eduskunta.fi-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-web.archive.org-39) As a result of the [1907 parliamentary elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1907_Finnish_parliamentary_election "1907 Finnish parliamentary election"), Finland's voters elected 19 women as the first female members of a representative parliament. This was one of many self-governing actions in the Russian autonomous province that led to conflict with the Russian governor of Finland, ultimately leading to the [creation of the Finnish nation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence_of_Finland "Independence of Finland") in 1917.

In the years before [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), women in Norway also won the right to vote. During WWI, Denmark, Russia (under the [Provisional Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Provisional_Government "Russian Provisional Government")), Germany, and Poland also recognized women's right to vote.

Canada gave right to vote to some women in 1917; women got the vote on the same basis as men in 1920, that is, men and women of certain races or status being excluded from voting until 1960, when universal adult suffrage was achieved.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-40)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/1930s_Gladys_Misick_Morrell_%26_Sergt_Henderson_%26_table_at_Cavello_Hill%2C_Bermuda.jpg/250px-1930s_Gladys_Misick_Morrell_%26_Sergt_Henderson_%26_table_at_Cavello_Hill%2C_Bermuda.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1930s_Gladys_Misick_Morrell_&_Sergt_Henderson_&_table_at_Cavello_Hill,_Bermuda.jpg)

A [Bermuda Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bermuda_Police_Service "Bermuda Police Service")[Sergeant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police_Sergeant "Police Sergeant") confiscates women's suffrage activist [Gladys Morrell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gladys_Morrell "Gladys Morrell")'s table in the 1930s.

The [Representation of the People Act 1918](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representation_of_the_People_Act_1918 "Representation of the People Act 1918") saw British women over 30 gain the vote. Dutch women won the passive vote (allowed to run for parliament) after a revision of the Dutch Constitution in 1917 and the active vote (electing representatives) in 1919, and American women on August 26, 1920, with the passage of the [19th Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "Nineteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution") (the [Voting Rights Act of 1965](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voting_Rights_Act_of_1965 "Voting Rights Act of 1965") secured voting rights for racial minorities). Irish women won the same voting rights as men in the [Irish Free State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Free_State "Irish Free State") constitution, 1922. In 1928, British women won suffrage on the same terms as men, that is, for ages 21 and older. The suffrage of Turkish women was introduced in 1930 for local elections and in 1934 for national elections.

By the time French women were granted the suffrage in July 1944 by [Charles de Gaulle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_Gaulle "Charles de Gaulle")'s government in exile, by a vote of 51 for, 16 against,[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-41) France had been for about a decade the only Western country that did not at least allow women's suffrage at municipal elections.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-42)

Voting rights for women were introduced into [international law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_law "International law") by the United Nations' Human Rights Commission, whose elected chair was [Eleanor Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleanor_Roosevelt "Eleanor Roosevelt"). In 1948 the United Nations adopted the [Universal Declaration of Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Declaration_of_Human_Rights "Universal Declaration of Human Rights"); Article 21 stated: "(1) Everyone has the right to take part in the government of his country, directly or through freely chosen representatives. (3) The will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government; this will shall be expressed in periodic and genuine elections which shall be by universal and equal suffrage and shall be held by secret vote or by equivalent free voting procedures."

The [United Nations General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly "United Nations General Assembly") adopted the [Convention on the Political Rights of Women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convention_on_the_Political_Rights_of_Women "Convention on the Political Rights of Women"), which went into force in 1954, enshrining the equal rights of women to vote, hold office, and access public services as set out by national laws.

### 21st century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Women%27s_suffrage&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 21st century")]

One of the most recent jurisdictions to acknowledge women's full right to vote was [Bhutan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhutan "Bhutan") in 2008 (its first national elections).[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-43) Most recently, King [Abdullah of Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdullah_of_Saudi_Arabia "Abdullah of Saudi Arabia"), after both national and international condemnation and activism by feminist groups, granted Saudi women the vote and right to run for office for the first time in the [2015 local elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Saudi_Arabian_municipal_elections "2015 Saudi Arabian municipal elections").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-photographtasneemalsultan,nationalgeographic-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-Stewart_2015-45)

## Suffrage movements

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Women%27s_suffrage&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Suffrage movements")]

See also: [Women's suffrage by country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage_by_country "Women's suffrage by country")

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Emmeline_Pankhurst_addresses_crowd.jpg/330px-Emmeline_Pankhurst_addresses_crowd.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Emmeline_Pankhurst_adresses_crowd.jpg)

After selling her home, British activist [Emmeline Pankhurst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmeline_Pankhurst "Emmeline Pankhurst") travelled constantly, giving speeches throughout Britain and the United States. One of her most famous speeches, _[Freedom or death](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Freedom%20or%20death "s:Freedom or death")_, was delivered in Connecticut in 1913.

The suffrage movement was a broad one, made up of women and men with a wide range of views. In terms of diversity, the greatest achievement of the 20th-century woman suffrage movement was its extremely broad class base.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-46) One major division, especially in Britain, was between suffragists, who sought to create change constitutionally, and [suffragettes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffragette "Suffragette"), led by English political activist [Emmeline Pankhurst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmeline_Pankhurst "Emmeline Pankhurst"), who in 1903 formed the more militant [Women's Social and Political Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Social_and_Political_Union "Women's Social and Political Union").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-47) Pankhurst would not be satisfied with anything but action on the question of women's enfranchisement, with "deeds, not words" the organization's motto.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-49)

[Elizabeth Cady Stanton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Cady_Stanton "Elizabeth Cady Stanton") and [Lucretia Mott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucretia_Mott "Lucretia Mott") were the first two women in America to organize the women's rights convention in July 1848. [Susan B. Anthony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_B._Anthony "Susan B. Anthony") later joined the movement and helped form the [National Woman Suffrage Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Woman_Suffrage_Association "National Woman Suffrage Association") (NWSA) in May 1869. Their goal was to change the 15th Amendment because it did not mention nor include women which is why the NWSA protested against it. Around the same time, there was also another group of women who supported the 15th amendment and they called themselves [American Woman Suffrage Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Woman_Suffrage_Association "American Woman Suffrage Association") (AWSA). The American Woman Suffrage Association was founded by [Lucy Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucy_Stone "Lucy Stone"), [Julia Ward Howe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia_Ward_Howe "Julia Ward Howe"), and [Thomas Wentworth Higginson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Wentworth_Higginson "Thomas Wentworth Higginson"), who were more focused on gaining access at a local level.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-National_Archives-2016-50) The two groups united became one and called themselves the National American Woman Suffrage Association (NAWSA).[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-National_Archives-2016-50)

Throughout the world, the [Women's Christian Temperance Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Christian_Temperance_Union "Women's Christian Temperance Union") (WCTU), which was established in the United States in 1873, campaigned for women's suffrage, in addition to ameliorating the condition of prostitutes.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage#cite_note-MarionOliver2014-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wo

Abstract: The introduction begins with a key aspect of the main theme: women’s political representation and its significance globally and then regionally in CEE. Women’s political representation is still a relatively new social phenomenon, despite the increased global visibility and presence of women leaders. Women did not win the right to vote and stand for office in most countries until the end of World War II, around 80 years ago. The State of Women’s Political Representation and Its Importance 

Women also trail men within the category of political representation in centers of political power. Globally, as of mid-2025, women make up 27% of national legislators around the world. 5 This means that just over one out of four legislators in the lower houses of national legislatures is a woman. Well over a century after suffrage was first secured in parts of the world, women are very far from being equally present actors in politics and, furthermore, the prospect of parity remains tenuous and uncertain. The projection made by UN Women, the leading women’s rights agency of the UN, is telling and concerning. Namely, if progress continues at the current rate in terms of women’s representation in politics, parity will not be achieved between men and women until 2063. 6 Indeed, it has been a slow and arduous road for gender equality activists and supportive politicians alike; often these actors challenge the status quo of masculinity in politics, only to see the already slow-moving hand of social progress challenged by fervent resistance and swift backlash. The activism of gender equality proponents has encountered challenges at almost every stage, and the current era is no exception. 

Backlash from “populist” forces, particularly more traditionally minded, right-wing movements, has contested gender equality gains in various national contexts. Populist supporters and actors have also reversed gains in others. For example, the judicial ruling of the Polish Constitutional Court in 2020 curtailed access to abortion, except in cases of rape, incest, or a threat to the pregnant woman’s life. This court decision was a direct result of the right-wing populist policies of a ruling party; specifically, the long-standing Polish Law and Justice Party ( Prawo i Sprawiedliwość; PiS), which governed Poland from 2015 to 2023. While in power, PiS “packed” the Polish Constitutional Court with its own loyalists, eventually ensuring the overturning of Poland’s previous and albeit conservative, but nonetheless, less restrictive abortion law. 

PiS eventually lost a pivotal 2023 national election to a more moderate and centrist party, the Civic Platform; but as of early 2026, the Polish abortion law has not been liberalized, due to continued opposition of members in the Polish Parliament, the Sejm. The Purpose of This Book 

This book explores the significant inroads women’s rights activists have made but also acknowledges the serious impediments that remain on the path to greater equality, particularly in politics. The focus of this book is specifically on nation-level legislatures and the women who enter them. While this is a relevant research site for all regions, this work explores the region of Central and Eastern Europe (CEE). This region is important to discuss because it includes many of the factors present in the world at large, factors that are promoting but also hindering the progress of women in politics. Women in this region have made strides in politics over time, as is discussed in greater detail in subsequent chapters. This has been especially significant since the fall of socialism, but their continued progress remains fragile, given the more oppositional forces actively working to assert a more traditional agenda in this part of the world. Studying the CEE region remains vital, particularly because it has been historically under-studied and at times misunderstood. The Region: Central and Eastern Europe 

For the purposes of this book, for general analysis, I include 19 countries in the region. The 19 countries I include are Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Czech Republic, Estonia, Hungary, Kosovo, Latvia, Lithu -

ania, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Poland, Romania, Serbia, Slovakia, Slovenia and Ukraine. These 19 countries do not represent an exhaustive list of Eastern European countries. They have instead been selected based on the following criteria: belonging to the general geographic area of Eastern Europe, having a level of electoral freedom that allows some kind of inter-party competition, and having a post-socialist status. 

Russia and Belarus are not included in this work because they do not meet the electoral competition requirements and therefore do not fulfill the minimum criteria for electoral freedom. They are therefore not appropriate cases for this kind of analysis of women in politics, which is partly dependent 19 intRoduC tion

Georgia and Armenia are also not included in this analysis because they are deemed outside the geographic scope of this book. They also face specific and unique challenges that would be better assessed in a work dedicated to their sub-region, which faces distinct challenges. 

Most of the case study countries are analyzed as a collective in the effort to generalize and make inferences across them. These broader analyses of the region mostly occur in chapters 2 (historical context) and 3 (a discussion of political representation). Three of the country cases, namely Serbia, Poland, and Moldova, are examined in greater detail as separate case studies in their own subsequent chapters. These countries were initially chosen because they all have a gender quota and have experienced a subsequent and steady increase in women in parliaments over time. Thus, they can provide a fruitful foundation for evaluating the effects of this numerical increase on other aspects of women’s political representation. They are also compelling cases not only in terms of history, but also in relation to their current geopolitical positions. The choice of cases follows the case study logic of diversity along various factors, namely more causal or independent ones. All three countries are CEE countries with a socialist past, but all have broader and divergent historical specificities and disparate realities based on respective spheres of influence that result in different domestic and foreign policy priorities. Poland is a former member of the Warsaw Pact and the country was the site of initial activism against the state socialist system in the early 1980s. Serbia is a post-conflict state, embroiled heavily in the breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s, which has seen a rise in authoritarianism since 2012, after a decade of implementing democratic and pro-EU reforms. Moldova is a former republic of the Soviet Union that, over the past three decades, has oscillated between pro-Russian and pro-European orientations. Thus, the cases have commonalities but are also very diverse, potentially leading to more information and associated discussion of the paths, challenges, setbacks, and victories of women leaders across the region.

Central and Eastern Europe in the Era of Durable Populism 

The countries of Central and Eastern Europe have seen a rise in right-wing populism in the second and third decades of the twenty-first century. Gains made by more progressive forces in the region have been challenged by those questioning the direction and utility of social progress and, by association, gender equality. Gender equality has become a widely accepted and frequently used term internationally. The term is related to efforts to narrow the gap in access and outcomes for men and women around the world. It is also a goal that is far from being met in any sector of society, even in advanced democracies. UN Women defines gender equality as: “… the equal rights, responsibilities and opportunities of women, men, girls and boys. Equality does not imply sameness but that the rights of women and men will not depend on the gender they were born with.” 11  Gender equality is often directly associated with women’s equality, although it refers to men also. Indeed, much of the gender-based discrimination still present in societies is directed toward women, although this is not always the case. Other populations, for example, LGBTQ+ people, face similar kinds of discrimination. Furthermore, women are certainly not a homogenous group: they have varied interests and different issues affect them. But it is the assumption of this work that gender equality in the political realm, at least, refers to closing the gap between men and women in terms of political access, representation, and power. Politics is still dominated by men across virtually all societies, and political gender equality is a goal that seeks to remedy this. Therefore, this work acknowledges various nuances in gender and gender equality but also recognizes that women share many commonalities in terms of the discrimination they face globally. Some of these challenges could be addressed and reduced by increasing their access to and presence in political power.

Foundational Ideas: Political Representation 

The focus of this work is situated in CEE, but it is based on extant knowledge on political representation. Hanna Pitkin’s seminal 1967 work, The Concept of Representation , discusses representation, which she defines simply as “making present in some sense something which is nevertheless not present literally or in fact.” 19  Political representation is tied to representing the electorate in spaces where they are not physically present. Representation is a key part of democratic accountability. If there is no direct link between the will of con -

stituencies, the people at large, and their political representatives, democracy ceases to function. Political representation ensures that the perspectives of people are heard and considered within decision-making bodies that have power and influence on said everyday lives. Political representation can take many forms, but representatives must be attuned to what their constituents want and need. This is related to the identity and actions of representatives. In this respect, Pitkin depicts political representation as being made up of three main categories: descriptive, substantive, and symbolic. Pitkin also puts forth a preceding category called “formalistic representation,” or rules and regulations that precede and initiate representation. 

The focus of this work is on descriptive, substantive, and symbolic representation because these kinds of representation have been linked to the literature on political representation more directly and have been discussed within the women and politics literature more readily. These three types of representation are essential for understanding how political representation works, especially in democracies, where representation and accountability are of critical importance and are often defined by state and constitutional design per se. Definitions of these kinds of representation have been developed over time. The definitions used in this work are mostly based on Pitkin’s initial definition of them and additional amendments that have been made to the definitions in later work. This original conceptual framework, although modified and contested over time, has given scholars useful tools to work with when assessing levels of political representation,

particularly that of previously marginalized or even excluded groups, including women but also racial and ethnic groups. 

Definitions of these kinds of representation are then important to broach. Descriptive representation, or “standing for” someone, is based on identity or how closely a representative “resembles” the group he or she (or they) is representing. For example, on some level, a woman descriptively repre -

sents other women by virtue of sharing that identity (assuming they both identify as women). Descriptive representation in academic literature has been associated with numerical representation. This aspect of descriptive representation of women has increased globally because the percentage of women in legislatures and politics has increased substantially over the past 25 years. This has been achieved due to the persistent activism of national and global feminist groups along with the resulting greater acceptance of gender equality norms among elite leaders and the public. 

Secondly, substantive representation, or “acting for,” refers to a representa -

tive acting on behalf of the interests of their represented group, with whom they often share an identity. For example, a woman discussing, introducing, or even sponsoring gender-sensitive legislation or legislation that furthers women’s interests as a group would involve her substantively representing other women. Notably, substantive representation has been conceptualized as occurring in two main ways. Franceschet and Piscopo argue that this kind of representation can be thought of as happening either by “process” or “outcome.” Substantive representation by “process” might entail women or representatives of other marginalized groups within legislatures in -

troducing, discussing, and debating legislation related to women’s issues, whereas representation by “outcome” entails getting legislation passed through a legislature. “Outcome” is thus linked to women politicians and their allies assuring that gender-conscious or gender equality legislation is passed as law. Franceschet and Piscopo argue that political representation occurs in both instances, even if in the case of process representation, no gender-conscious legislation is passed. They note: “Transforming political practices and winning new policies are certainly commendable instances of substantive representation as outcome, though they are not necessary for representation itself to occur.” 20  Certainly, the efforts of women in politics to raise awareness of women’s issues, such as reproductive rights, violence against women, sexual harassment, literacy, access to education, inter alia , is

Often these initiatives are spearheaded by groups that have a direct connection to them and a vested interest in their adoption. 

The country case studies of this book document and analyze the pro -

cesses behind legislative action in CEE countries: the advocacy women in CEE politics engage in in legislatures to make their societies more gender equal. This book includes examples of women introducing or advocating for legislation in CEE that directly benefits or at least relates to women, thus recognizing the importance of “process.” Women-led initiatives that were passed by parliaments or congresses within CEE countries are emphasized, because these efforts are emblematic of substantive progress, although “pro -

cess” based efforts, as noted, are equally necessary in this larger picture of advocacy. While both kinds of substantive representation matter, “outcome” representation can give us a clear and more direct sense of what is being done and by whom to aid women’s causes. The fate of proposed policies can also shed light on not only how far women have come in certain legislatures in terms of influencing the policy agenda, but also what kinds of challenges they face in the process. In a key sense, substantive representation is linked to the theme of this book and the findings from this research speak back to its core message: while women in CEE have made strides, as evidenced by their many efforts to change and pass existing laws, significant impediments remain and sometimes hinder them from making sustainable and lasting policy changes and reforms. 

Lastly, symbolic representation refers to the kinds of responses repre -

sentatives produce in groups with whom they share an identity. A woman representative who inspires other women to run for political office is an example of symbolic representation in practice, as her presence in politics has elicited a commitment and motivation from other women to be politi -

cally active. This is widely known as “the role model effect”. Measuring and ascertaining symbolic representation has often proven difficult in practice, however. The sections on symbolic representation in each case study chapter focus on the public perception of women in politics, in addition to public perception of key women’s issues, such as reproductive rights. The thinking behind symbolic representation is that an increase in the presence of women in politics can not only transform perceptions of women’s capabilities and belonging within politics, but also potentially transform perceptions of other, related issues, such as government efficiency and levels of corruption. The sections on symbolic representation in the case study chapters embody this 28  WomEn’s PolitiCal REPREsEntation in CEntRal and EastERn EuRoPE 

logic but also connect symbolic representation with the transformation or changes in attitudes towards women’s issues such as abortion (Poland), but also LGBTQ+ rights (Serbia) and EU membership (Moldova), assuming that symbolic representation can also involve electorates responding to the causes women leaders champion or even symbolize in more open and positive ways. Since symbolic representation has not been readily explored in the CEE region, the sections on this kind of representation are preliminary and broad, using public surveys to gauge changes in public onion across themes. 

Political representation as initially introduced by Pitkin has been a central preoccupation of many scholars of women and politics. In general, scholars have linked increases in descriptive representation with greater levels of substantive representation, although this connection does not appear in every context studied. Women make up a much larger portion of the parliaments and congresses in the CEE region than ever before, but this increase in descriptive representation has not always led to progressive changes in policy and a transformation of public perception in key areas, as the chapters elaborate. 

Guiding Frameworks in the Field of Women and Politics 

The women and politics literature has burgeoned over the past several decades. Seminal works in the field have covered significant themes related to the increasing presence of women in politics. As the number of women in the political realm has increased, so has the scholarly attention to this theme. The literature in this field has progressed through different eras. Earlier works in this important subfield of political science focused on the descriptive or numerical aspects of women in politics. Scholars such as Mansbridge 21  and Phillips 22  asserted that including more women in politics was a matter of just and equitable representation in democratic settings but they also noted the non-linear aspects of this connection, i.e. not all women are the same. Thinkers have also argued that having more women in politics is necessary because women politicians can understand the experiences of other women in a more authentic and direct way than male politicians can. They can, in turn, represent the interests and issues of women in a more comprehensive and responsive way.

Eventually, the literature on increasing the presence of women and politics became linked to the literature on gender quotas. Gender quotas are tools that countries and political parties use to increase the number of women in political institutions, most frequently legislatures, such as parliaments and congresses. Gender quotas have been instrumental in increasing the percentage of women in parliaments across national contexts. Currently, 

over 130 countries use some kind of gender quota. 23  This number has grown substantially since the 1980s, when gender quotas existed in only a handful of countries, including many in the CEE region. The early gender quota literature initially documented different kinds of quotas and weighed their efficacy. 

The typology of quotas has expanded over time. Gender quotas come in three main forms: legislated quotas, voluntary party quotas, and reserved seats. Legislated quotas are legal quotas that are enshrined in a country’s constitution or electoral law. They often mandate a minimum percentage of women that must appear on a political party’s electoral list, such as 30% or even 40%. Voluntary party quotas are quotas that political parties adopt in their respective party statutes. Generally, these quotas also call for a minimum percentage of women to be placed on electoral lists. Voluntary party quotas are just that, voluntary or optional, and are not always used by every party in the national political system. The first voluntary party quota was used in Norway in the early 1970s. Scandinavian countries, namely Sweden, Denmark, and Norway, are pioneers in women’s political representation and the early utilization of party gender quotas. The resulting higher levels of women’s political representation in those countries are linked to their early and successful efforts to aid political gender equality. Reserved seats are quotas that generally allocate a percentage of seats in parliament to women. Sometimes, these quotas also designate several electoral districts where only women can run, especially in majoritarian systems. For decades, Rwanda, an East African country with a tragic recent past and an increasingly authoritarian government, has been the world’s leader in terms of women in politics. Most notably, it is the world’s leader in the percentage of women in parliament, and it uses reserved seats, as do many countries in the Global South. Overall, legislated quotas are the most frequently used quota and the most effective. 

The quota literature first explored why countries adopt quotas at all. This was a relevant question, given that most parliaments were (and still

The rise of anti-gender ideologies across disparate regions, including CEE, has led to heightened levels of harassment and other kinds of violence directed towards women. Many core and leading concepts have come out of this pioneering literature, again mostly situated in a Western context. The Research Approach 

This book first contextualizes the theme of women on politics in CEE by providing a brief history of women’s political representation in the region. It then discusses the different types of political representation in greater detail and how these kinds of political representation have occurred (or not) in CEE. The book portrays a larger and more comprehensive picture of the status of women in politics in the region in the first few chapters. Later, it focuses on three more in-depth representative country case studies: Serbia, Poland, and Moldova. Case studies are useful methodological tools for this kind of study as they allow for a bounded and deeper exploration of the relevant contexts of a larger study. As the examples are restricted and manageable qualitatively, the work can explore and compare all cases

In terms of data collection, the book primarily relies on original (primary) and secondary research. The guiding frameworks have been derived from the existing literature on women in politics, which, as noted, have mostly come from studies on Western nations. The authors of that work found that many aspects of women in politics in Western Europe were also present in Eastern Europe, including encouraging features of electoral systems, such as proportional representation, and challenges to promoting women in politics, such as male-dominated incumbency. Outline of Chapters 

This book has seven chapters. Chapter 1 is this introduction. Chapter 2 presents a historical overview of women in politics in the CEE region. It discusses the history of women’s political representation in CEE from the beginnings of the suffrage era through the present day. This chapter empha -

sizes the state socialist period as a defining era for women in politics in the CEE region, almost indirectly so. The system is hereby called “state socialism” because full communism, as envisioned by Karl Marx, was never attained as an end goal in any CEE state. Socialism is thus a more accurate descriptor. By granting women certain fundamental rights, like the right to vote and the right to divorce, and by encouraging women to advance themselves economically and professionally, socialist governments contributed to the social empowerment of women, although the transformative effect of this remained very limited at that time. Those socialist governments, by design, were mostly led by Politburos, or executive arms of the Communist Party. So even when women were present in socialist-era legislatures, they were not generally influential in deciding on or enacting relevant laws and policies, as women were generally absent from Politburos. 

The history of women in politics in this region is also tied to the history of gender quotas, which at the time promoted women’s inclusion in socialist parliaments. Many countries in CEE, including the Soviet Union itself, used socialist-era gender or women’s quotas to promote women’s political representation. Many countries had a significant portion of women in their parliaments, despite the limitations of these women’s actual legisla -

tive power. However, when CEE countries removed gender quotas upon democratization, the descriptive representation of women fell in a stunning fashion, from over 30% in some countries to under 10% in many countries after the fall of  socialism. 30  This drop is a significant part of the history of women in politics in CEE, and it is discussed at greater length in chapter 2. It provides a historical overview of this theme in the region and important contextual information that will be relevant for subsequent chapters. Ad -

ditionally, chapter 2 emphasizes the recent history in CEE, namely the rise of right-wing populism and its effects on women’s rights and women’s political representation. The chapter argues that the combination of the lingering legacies of socialism and the current political and social challenges in the region have made the road to and life within politics arduous for women in CEE.

Looking Forward 

The state of women’s political representation is a worthy goal, but it is also an important part of supporting and improving democracy. Including women’s perspectives and, of course, the perspectives of all other marginal -

ized groups, is a core part of democratic ideals and justice, not to mention a significant component of a functioning and accountable democracy. With the rise of anti-democratic sentiments in the world, it is crucial to explore the level of women’s political representation to ensure attention is paid to this theme and it is recognized as a valid and constituent part of accountable politics. Right-wing populism opposes many aspects of more progressive gender equality initiatives and is an ongoing threat to women’s political advancement. Its rise is particularly pronounced in CEE, and it remains a problem for more moderate voices in the region. Exploring the intersection of these timely themes remains significant. Through a discussion of the region’s past and present in terms of women in politics, this work discusses developments related to three main types of political representation a first put forth by Pitkin. It is argued that although women 37 intRoduC tion 

have made significant strides in the CEE region over time, their continued progress has not been straightforward or unopposed, despite their many laudable and often effective efforts. The future of equality also remains unguaranteed, especially given the uncertain reality women in politics face. The promise of progress remains present, but stubborn realities—rooted in deep, historical legacies and situated in the tumult of the contemporary political era—threaten this path to sustained progress. What follows is an in-depth discussion of the theme of women in politics in CEE and the long journey that remains to arrive at true parity, in an ever-changing era and a similarly dynamic region. 2.  The Past as Present? The History of Women in Politics in Central and Eastern Europe 

Abstract: Chapter 2 provides the historical context for the book. The chapter traces the history of women’s political representation in CEE from the early twentieth century (the era of suffrage activism), to the era of women in politics during state socialism, and finally to the status of women in politics now. Gender quotas are first discussed within the era of state socialism and then presented as a central tool for the recommit -

ment to gender equality in the CEE region now. The chapter argues that historical legacies remain, including aspects of state socialism, and also the deleterious effects of socialism’s rapid decline. 

Keywords: women’s suffrage in CEE; state socialism; rise of right-wing populism; authoritarianism; gender quotas 

Women’s political representation in Central and Eastern Europe (CEE) has aspects in common with the general path of women’s involvement in politics globally. Women in many CEE countries initially fought for the right to vote and to run for office, as did women internationally. Notably, some of this activism occurred before the rise of socialism in the region, and some of it occurred during socialism, as suffrage was granted in most CEE countries by the 1950s. Activism for gender-equality causes also continues today, decades after the collapse of the state socialist system. Political opportunities for activism in historical periods also played a crucial part in this trajectory. Women took on more substantial roles outside the family and entered the public space as workers, during and after World War I and World War II. These political openings mirrored the experiences of women in the Western

Divergent Paths to Suffrage: Women in Politics in CEE 

For women in the CEE region, the fight for suffrage, or the right to vote in elections (passive suffrage), and the associated right to run for office (active suffrage), overlapped temporally and substantively with the fight for suffrage in other parts of the world. The beginning of the global suffrage movement is often associated with women’s activism in Anglophone countries. The first country to grant women the right to vote and run for office was New Zealand, in 1893. 2 Activism for suffrage in the English-speaking world, in particular the United Kingdom and later the United States, defined this important era and propelled other women’s movements to fight for this foundational human right. Activists paved the way for women to organize and advocate for an expansion of rights in many CEE countries, where women’s organizations came into existence in the second half of the nineteenth century, coinciding with the rise of women’s suffrage activism in the Western world. 3

In contrast, when women gained the right to vote in the Soviet Union in 1918, it was not solely the result of grassroots women’s activism, but mostly because of the tenets of socialism. Socialism was implemented in Russia after the 1917 Revolution, which overthrew a monarchy, that of the Russian Tsar Nikolai II, by assassinating him and members of his immediate family. This revolution came to be known as the Bolshevik Revolution. The Bolshevik Revolution’s leader, Vladimir Lenin, and other contemporary socialists in the Soviet Union, primarily believed in the economic potential and value of women. Their vision for a socialist state and an ultimately socialist world included the progress of women, mostly because women were viewed as equal and crucial members of the proletariat, or the working class. Socialists believed economic empowerment would aid women’s emancipation and the promotion and growth of communism as originally envisioned by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels. As Ghodsee and Mead note: “In theory, socialism would free women from patriarchal domination by educating them and fully incorporating them into the paid labor force.” 4

This top-down nature of socialist states affected how politics were practiced and the effect of votes in practice. Women’s Political Representation During the Era of Limited Suffrage 

Once women attained the right to vote and the associated right to run for office, they were formally able to participate in politics, at least to an extent. However, the early era of women’s political involvement did not yield many women in pre-socialist legislatures, as one could expect at that time. For the most part, women’s political representation in the inter-war period remained very low. Women’s political representation in any legislature never exceeded 7% during that era. 11  It is notable that women were present at all, however, given the political and societal constraints of the time. While there were some women in these early legislatures, generally there were too few for meaningful solidarity. Their ability to effect change was also limited, given, among other impediments, the unsteady environments of their countries at the time, in the turbulent inter-war period of European history. The opportunities for any politician to effect change in these nascent democratic legislatures were limited by the lack of time and continuity. By the late 1930s, many of these legislatures had been dissolved because of the beginning of WWII and resulting foreign, in many cases Nazi German, occupations. By 1939, the chaos of war commenced on the European continent. In the devastating aftermath of WWII and in some cases years after, CEE countries adopted a socialist government, and their system of political representation dramatically changed. The reality for women in CEE also shifted, ushering in an era where women made some progress, albeit in a context of significant political and societal constraints. 

Women’s Political Representation in CEE During State Socialism 

The Larger Context 

By the end of WWII, many states within CEE adopted a state socialist system. These systems were formed in the wake of the gruesomeness and vast destruction of WWII. In some CEE countries, including Yugoslavia, socialist movements were driven by grassroots “indigenous” efforts. Many pro-socialist or pro-democratic movements in the region fought against fascist occupation during WWII. The partisan resistance of Yugoslavia, for example, fought on two ideological fronts: against the fascist occupy -

ing forces in several parts of the country and against the nationalist or

monarchist forces also vying for power, such as the “Chetniks” of  Serbia. 12 

The reality for CEE countries post-WWII mirrored the reality of much of Europe at that time. WWII devastated the entire continent, claiming millions of lives and destroying vast infrastructure, while reshaping the priorities of past and new leaders and dramatically changing the political realities of its citizens. 

Notably, Europe became separated by a symbolic but powerful divide, famously coined the “Iron Curtain” and represented by the Berlin Wall, which demarcated East Germany from the West. The eastern part of the continent fell under the sphere of influence of the Soviet Union. For the most part, Western Europe retained a capitalist and, in some cases, corresponding democratic system (other countries had totalitarian or fascist governments, such as Francisco Franco’s fascist regime in Spain, the effects of which lasted well into the 1980s). Socialist governments in CEE were generally collective in nature; they banned or severely limited private property, employed government-controlled economies, and discouraged private enterprise and free market determination of supply and demand, thereby determining the price of goods and services. Politically, in most countries, the socialist-era Politburo, determined policy. Parliaments existed but generally “rubber-stamped” the directives of the government. The media was censored and state media was central to spreading news. Education was generally free at all levels, however, and housing was often granted by the government, which developed and owned most property. Robust social welfare programs existed, such as childcare, healthcare, and pensions. Political dissent was tolerated at times and punished in other eras, also varying by  country. 13 

Within the state socialist region of Europe, women also faced a new and complex reality. In many CEE countries during the era of state socialism, women were granted more substantial rights. For example, women in several CEE countries had reproductive rights, such as the right to an abortion. Additionally, women were encouraged to attain higher levels of education, including at the secondary and tertiary levels, and education was mostly free and accessible for all people. Socialist governments also granted longer maternity leaves and sometimes free childcare and child stipends. Women were also encouraged to pursue politics, as quotas were implemented in various countries across CEE, including the Soviet Union itself. In general, women’s roles in society expanded from the mostly private to the newly

However, the lived reality proved less promising for many women in this era. While some of this may have also been the case in the democratic or Western world, unlike women in the West, women in CEE could not generally organize themselves against the state to raise awareness about this problem. governments in power, with some exceptions. 17  Thus, the overall context for women’s political representation was limited. While the socialist state offered some basis for women to enter public life, its priorities were not in line with more advanced feminist goals. The state’s emphasis on workers’ rights rather than gender equality itself, coupled with the state’s non-democratic organization, limited the space for women’s political representation and activism within politics and beyond. The general intolerance of dissent and grassroots efforts also curbed the efforts of women to advocate for their causes. Therefore, while women attained greater equality, broadly conceived, during socialism, the state system was not conducive to ensuring more far-reaching and sustainable progress.

Gender Quotas and Women in Politics During Socialism 

Gender quotas were used in the state socialist system before they were used in many parts of the Western world. Voluntary party quotas were first used in Norway in the early 1970s, whereas quotas in the socialist world appeared earlier, such as in the 1930s in the Soviet Union. Some of these quotas took the form of informal quotas, as they were a part of the policy approach of many of these socialist states. The Soviet Union used formal gender quotas to bolster the number of women in their “soviets” or local  legislatures. 18 

Other countries, such as Yugoslavia, never used formal gender quotas but instead promoted women in politics informally, especially after the new constitution of 1974. 19  Despite this diversity in adoption and implementation, all CEE state socialist countries promoted greater inclusion of women in politics, despite the structural constraints that otherwise existed in the socialist system. Most countries therefore used gender quotas to include more women in politics. Socialist countries also used quotas in different areas of labor and life, but rarely did these efforts produce serious gender equality reform or even touch the epicenters of governmental power. 

As Dahlerup and Antić Gaber (2017) write: 

The fact is that under communism/socialism there were many different quota systems at work in various countries, and that quotas were installed not just for women, but also for workers, youth and other groups. At the same time, there were no quota provisions for the highest male-dominated decision-making bodies, which in many cases only had one token woman. Several studies also show that the share of women in important political bodies was not sufficiently high at any of the various levels of political decision making. The situation even worsened after the fall of the socialist/communist regimes, and women almost disappeared 

entirely from politics. 20

CEE Transitions to Democracy and Women’s Political Representation 

Gender quotas were a casualty of democratic transitions in CEE during the 1990s. When elections became competitive and free in the region, new democratic governments abandoned existing quotas, viewing them as relics of the old state system and incompatible with democratic elections and the perceived and associated values of a democratic meritocracy and “pure” competition. Gender equality initiatives in general were not prioritized at the time. What became paramount was the transition to democracy and capitalism, and in diverse countries across CEE this transition was far from smooth or ultimately equitable. Across Decades: The Waxing and Waning of Women’s Political Representation in CEE 

The story of women’s political representation in CEE is one of full of nadirs and zeniths, with many factors associated with these sometimes stark and lingering changes. Since achieving a very high percentage of women in socialist legislatures pre-transitions to democracy, CEE countries took a long time to recommit themselves to the cause of political gender equality. This is reflected in the state of numerical representation of women in parliaments across three decades, represented in the figure below.
