Women were well-represented in socialist legislatures, but this level of representation dropped significantly upon transitions to democracy in the region. The level of political representation for women began to increase again steadily in the mid-2000s to now. While this recommitment to gender equality and resulting numerical increase of women in parliament are promising signs for the future, this development has not guaranteed an improvement in other kinds of representation, including substantive and symbolic. Additionally, the region is facing a right-wing populist backlash, 58  WomEn’s PolitiCal REPREsEntation in CEntRal and EastERn EuRoPE 

whose ideology and aims often target gender equality initiatives. While gender quotas themselves have not been directly rescinded in any CEE country, right-wing populist forces have attacked other aspects of gender equality programs. Examples of this abound in the region. More notably, during his time in power, the long-serving Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and his political party, Fidesz, targeted gender studies programs and have curtailed the activism of LGBTQ+ advocacy groups and other NGOs. Similarly, during its time in power in Poland, the Law and Justice Party (PiS) also curtailed women’s rights, most notably the right to an abortion. 

Despite numerical gains, women’s political representation in the region stands in a precarious place, mostly because of current geopolitical factors but also historical legacies. The hegemonic influence of an autocratic and increasingly isolated Russia is part of this current reality. Russia, like other authoritarian regimes, exports its own worldview to the regional and global stage, and this view of the world differs markedly from the previous one held during state socialism, despite both having ambitions beyond the state itself. This new approach is rooted in a primarily masculinist, expansionary, and ultimately regressive approach, one that lionizes force and historical and mythical glory. Many CEE countries, given that they exist within this realm of influence, are therefore dealing with significant external pressures and in some cases are forced to take difficult positions about their allegiances and ultimately their political priorities. 

Concurrently, there are more positive influences for the cause of gender equality. Most importantly, the counterinfluence of the European Union (EU) has been mostly constructive for many candidate countries (e.g., Serbia, Albania, Montenegro, North Macedonia, and Moldova) as they work to reform significant aspects of their laws and policies to align with EU law— the acquis communautaire . The norms the EU has “diffused” to candidate countries has encouraged them to strengthen their commitment to gender equality and, by extension, this has encouraged candidate countries to collaborate with the EU on crucial regional and global issues. Even the conversations and efforts related to gender quota adoption were influenced by EU norms and standards. Many groups vying for these reforms pointed to the spirit of the EU and its own values to convince lawmakers to adopt gender quotas. Furthermore, the quota adoption process in many countries involved persistent efforts and a substantial amount of organizing and social movement pressure, most often from women’s groups themselves. 

However, several countries in the region do not have gender quotas in any form, so there is no guarantee that the gains in women’s political representation will be sustained over time. In some countries, gender quotas 59 thE Past as PREsEnt? 

have been rejected by legislatures and even the public, partly due to the association of quotas with the “Soviet” or, more accurately, the imposing aspects of the state socialist past. Unfortunately, quotas have long been associated with a diminishment of meritocracy in politics, but in the political arenas of most countries in the world, the best candidates cannot always run in elections, let alone win, often due to the legacy of corruption, stifling of dissent, and other associated legacies of entrenched power. Therefore, pure meritocracies do not always exist in this realm. Given the currently pervasive and historically omnipresent levels of gender discrimination worldwide, quotas are one solution for reducing the inequality of women in political realms, as has been demonstrated by the progress in CEE. Quotas have helped this cause even in the CEE context, regardless of the otherwise challenging environment for gender equality efforts. But even for quotas, resistance in the region is sometimes pronounced and cannot always be countered by appeals to higher authorities, such as the European Union. The EU can recommend the promotion of gender equality and even mandate some of it directly through the acquis, but it cannot and does not require candidate countries to adopt gender quotas. The adoption of quotas is therefore a mostly domestic concern and requires domestic activism and broader public and elite-level support. 

CEE History as Foundational and Its Effects as Ongoing 

This historical chapter on CEE women in politics has discussed several eras of this umbrella theme. The chapter first explored the suffrage era in the region and its effects on women’s political representation. While there were many suffrage activists across CEE countries that helped secure the right to vote for women, even before WWII, much of their legacy was lost in the subsequent historical developments of the region. While the state socialist systems that arose after WWII employed their own versions of political gender equality, these systems were run mostly from the top down, and gender equality grassroots activism became obsolete, mostly because this kind of activism was forbidden or discouraged by new socialist governments. Even though women’s political representation increased in this system numerically, the effects of this were mostly “cosmetic” as virtually no legislator in this system could introduce or even advocate for meaningful reforms. Decisions were generally made in socialist Politburos and not in respective national parliaments. 60  WomEn’s PolitiCal REPREsEntation in CEntRal and EastERn EuRoPE 

However, government initiatives in the socialist era helped women to an extent. Gender quotas enabled many women to enter socialist-era parliaments, thus enabling a generation of women to participate in this otherwise masculine realm. But upon the transition to democracy in the early 1990s, socialist-era gender quotas were abandoned by all CEE states. It would take two decades for countries to truly re-embrace gender quotas and reattain previous levels of women’s political representation. As this chapter notes, it was this effort to readopt gender quotas that eventually increased the percentage of women in CEE parliaments to the current level of close to 30%, which is above the world average. This chapter also provided historical context related to the broader theme of women in politics in CEE by discussing several eras that influenced the women in contemporary politics. While women were viewed as equals in the proletarian struggle during socialism, they were still expected to act according to traditional norms in the private sphere. Socialism did not do enough to change attitudes in this private realm. This lack of progress is also reinforced in the reality women face today, with heightened backlash stemming from right-wing populist narratives that emphasize women’s roles as mostly belonging to the private sphere. This chapter argues that women’s political representation in CEE was defined by unique but also universal circumstances. Like many women in the world, CEE women used the opportunities available to them to further their gender equality goals. Without their efforts, the region would not be even as equal as it is today.

The concept of political representation has preoccupied political philoso -

phers and scholars for a very long time, in both direct and indirect ways. Although ancient Greek texts did not deal directly with the concept of representation (as the actual practice of it was limited in that era), the work of philosophers at that time remains relevant for discussions of democracy and by extension, representation of the demos , or the people. Aristotle’s thinking on the polity and what it means to be a good citizen and live the “good life” set a foundation for more contemporary discussions of

After all, political representatives are supposed to “represent,” and, by extension, “stand for” their constituents. They also are, or at least should be, held accountable for their choices and actions. What this means and how it works vary greatly across temporal, political, and national contexts. 

Scholars, including Hanna Pitkin herself, trace more modern interpreta -

tions of political representation to the work of English philosopher Thomas Hobbes, who wrote his seminal works in the seventeenth century and whose treatise The Leviathan is one of the most influential texts in the field of classical political science. The Leviathan is a work that discusses basic social organization, and it maintains that a social contract is necessary between people and governments to enforce necessary order and diminish natural chaos. Absolute freedom is exchanged between a government and its citizens for a set of laws and rules that make existence more stable and ultimately endurable. Life in the “state of nature” is too “nasty, brutish and short” to facilitate meaningful existence, therefore a strong “sovereign” is needed to enforce laws. 1 Hobbes’s work argues that humans need to overcome their “primitive” states of nature, and this tenet remains foundational for much of political philosophy, even influencing the field of international relations, whose scholars use Hobbes’s concept of a “state of nature” to describe the international realm, where an “anarchy,” or absence of a central government, exists to this day. 2

However, Hobbes’s original work has limitations for the concept of political representation in our modern era. His idea of representation as needing to be “absolute” because a populace generally authorizes a repre -

sentative to represent them absolutely is problematic because it proposes an anti-democratic view of representing citizens. Pitkin, in response to Hobbes, calls for a different kind of political representation that authorizes a representative to “stand for” and “act for” a group, but not in absolute terms and not without due consideration of the group’s priorities and interests. Indeed, political representation, to Pitkin and in more ideal terms, should involve more deliberate and collaborative or at least cooperative aspects.

Political representation, just like democracy itself, has, as a concept, been expanded over time. Hobbes’s view of political representation was just the start. Political philosophers and scholars of the field have refined this concept over time to make it more applicable to and useful for the contemporary era. Most relevantly for this work, Pitkin reinforces this idea of what representation is and contributes other core concepts to this theme. She introduces four main types of representation in practice—formalistic, descriptive, substantive, and symbolic representation—and delineates what they are and how they they function. Formalistic representation partly refers to the rules of elections, how representatives are chosen. Electoral laws and procedures vary across national contexts. Surely, the way elections are organized is crucial for political representation. For example, having a parliamentary system with proportional representation rather than a majoritarian system affects the way people are represented in a country. In the US, the absence of a third party marginalizes people who do not identify with either major party, leaving them with fewer options at the voting booth. European democracies, on the other hand, often have smaller political parties in their parliaments that represent unique, nuanced, and often avant-garde viewpoints of the populace. Parliamentary systems therefore generally offer more options to voters, even though power also resides within larger and longer-standing, mainstream parties. Rules and procedures are thus important aspects of representation to document and examine. 

However, Pitkin’s work offers other more useful terms and concepts that have been discussed by scholars much more directly and thoroughly. Indeed, the remaining three types of representation have been given much more attention, especially in the literature about women and politics. Descriptive representation, which refers to how well a representative “resembles” their constituents in terms of identity markers (e.g., gender, race, class), has greatly influenced the literature on the representation of women. The idea is that the more closely a representative resembles his or her constituency according to identity characteristics, the better the representative can represent his or her constituents. Pitkin called this “standing for” a group. This concept has been used by women and politics scholars to argue for an increase in women’s political representation. 3 Presumably, women representatives identify with women constituents more strongly than men and therefore can represent

The concept of descriptive representation is linked to subsequent “substantive representation,” or what Pitkin linked to “acting for.” In this type of representation, representatives who share a common identity with a group are expected to advocate for said group through the promotion of certain values and beliefs and associated policies that could further that group’s interests and improve their quality of life. Women and politics scholars have also used this proposed connection in their research. It is thought that women, especially once they attain a significant presence in legislatures, begin to advocate for women’s interests and issues. But this assertion remains contested in the literature, and in practice it is not always so linear. 4

There is also the concept of symbolic representation, which refers to the ability of representatives to act as transformative symbols for groups they represent. Namely, the presence of certain representatives in a political body can evoke feelings among voters or constituents, and can potentially change perceptions and attitudes, and even inspire different thinking or action among those represented. Examples of this would be an increase in women in parliament changing the public’s perception of women as politicians or the parliament itself, as to view them more favorably. Another example is the increase of women in a political body inspiring more women to vie for positions within this institution, again called “the role model effect”. Women and politics scholars have also used this concept to evaluate the effects of increased descriptive representation of women on perceptions of women in politics. These studies have generally shown a positive association between the two types of representation that emphasize “standing for” in different ways. Descriptive representation and symbolic representation are therefore linked; while descriptive representation emphasizes shared identity as being a conduit for better representation within institutions, symbolic representation emphasizes shared identity as being a part of a change in public perception and eventually broader societal change. 

This work recognizes all three types of political representation as being important, but it argues that descriptive representation, or increasing the presence of marginalized groups, is often a necessary, but perhaps insuf -

ficient, precursor for the rest. Substantive representation, while significant, is generally facilitated by the increased presence of previously excluded groups in political institutions. Fundamental Presence: The Descriptive Representation of Women 

The concerning underrepresentation of women and other marginalized groups in many parliaments and congresses around the world throughout much of the twentieth century encouraged scholars and activists alike to pursue meaningful reforms and policies that could remedy this persistent social problem. As previously discussed, state socialist governments in Europe were among the first to introduce gender quotas in their legislatures. Scandinavian states were among the first to adopt voluntary party quotas in the 1970s. But it was not until the early 1990s and the democratization of Latin America that new democracies (or any democracies at all) began to adopt legislated quotas that made the inclusion of women on electoral 66  WomEn’s PolitiCal REPREsEntation in CEntRal and EastERn EuRoPE 

lists mandatory for political parties. It was also at this time that political gender equality began to become an international goal or priority. This was mostly a result of global women’s activism. 

The United Nations became a key forum for the transmission of gender equality goals and strategies. The UN hosted four women’s conferences between 1975 and 1995, and the last one (the 1995 Beijing Conference) was the most well-attended and influential. These conferences brought together women’s groups from diverse regions in the world. Each conference ended with a report and a series of gender equality targets for the next meeting. There has not been a meeting since 1995, but every five years, women’s activists revisit the Beijing Platform at the United Nations during the annual meetings of the Commission on the Status of Women and assess progress and set goals for the future. This international framework has contributed to the promotion of women in politics as the Beijing Platform, most notably, included the advancement of women’s political representation as a stated goal for the future. Literature concerning women’s political representation also burgeoned in the 1990s. As the state socialist systems collapsed in many parts of the world, democracy became the ideal regime type of the time. This historical development created an increasing awareness and openness to international norms and standards, including gender equality. Certainly, earlier feminist writers, including Simone de Beauvoir, raised awareness about the inclusion of women decades prior to this time, but the momentum of the day seemed to favor not only increasing activism concerning women’s rights, but also more scholarship dedicated to it.

The logical first step for scholars was to discuss descriptive representation or, in practical terms, increasing the number of women in legislatures around the world. Pitkin suggests that representatives who share an identity with a group can represent said group more authentically, but not all scholars agree. Some argue that even if women share a common gender identity, they do not by default share the same interests or positions. This makes it very difficult to articulate a common vision or position for all women. In turn, scholars such as Phillips 5 and Mansbridge 6 argue that women representatives can represent women’s issues effectively without essentializing or homogenizing

Abstract: The introduction begins with a key aspect of the main theme: women’s political representation and its significance globally and then regionally in CEE. The conceptual framework, based on the seminal work of Pitkin, is presented. The methodology, research approach and their appropriateness for this project are discussed. This is followed by a brief overview of all subsequent chapters. 

Keywords: descriptive representation; substantive representation; symbolic representation; gender equality 

Women’s political representation is still a relatively new social phenomenon, despite the increased global visibility and presence of women leaders. Women did not win the right to vote and stand for office in most countries until the end of World War II, around 80 years ago. After pioneering efforts of women activists in the Anglophone world secured the right to vote (passive suffrage) and the right to run for political office (active suffrage) around the beginning of the twentieth century (e.g., New Zealand [1893], the United Kingdom [1918], and later the United States [1920]), other countries followed suit. But the cascade of suffrage commenced mostly after the end of World War II. At this pivotal point in world history, previous governments collapsed, colonies were freed from colonial rule, and new constitutions were written. 1 These historical

The State of Women’s Political Representation and Its Importance 

Women also trail men within the category of political representation in centers of political power. Globally, as of mid-2025, women make up 27% of national legislators around the world. 5 This means that just over one out of four legislators in the lower houses of national legislatures is a woman. Well over a century after suffrage was first secured in parts of the world, women are very far from being equally present actors in politics and, furthermore, the prospect of parity remains tenuous and uncertain. The projection made by UN Women, the leading women’s rights agency of the UN, is telling and concerning. Namely, if progress continues at the current rate in terms of women’s representation in politics, parity will not be achieved between men and women until 2063. 6 Indeed, it has been a slow and arduous road for gender equality activists and supportive politicians alike; often these actors challenge the status quo of masculinity in politics, only to see the already slow-moving hand of social progress challenged by fervent resistance and swift backlash. The activism of gender equality proponents has encountered challenges at almost every stage, and the current era is no exception. 

Backlash from “populist” forces, particularly more traditionally minded, right-wing movements, has contested gender equality gains in various national contexts. Populist supporters and actors have also reversed gains in others. For example, the judicial ruling of the Polish Constitutional Court in 2020 curtailed access to abortion, except in cases of rape, incest, or a threat to the pregnant woman’s life. This court decision was a direct result of the right-wing populist policies of a ruling party; specifically, the long-standing Polish Law and Justice Party ( Prawo i Sprawiedliwość; PiS), which governed Poland from 2015 to 2023. While in power, PiS “packed” the Polish Constitutional Court with its own loyalists, eventually ensuring the overturning of Poland’s previous and albeit conservative, but nonetheless, less restrictive abortion law. 

PiS eventually lost a pivotal 2023 national election to a more moderate and centrist party, the Civic Platform; but as of early 2026, the Polish abortion law has not been liberalized, due to continued opposition of members in the Polish Parliament, the Sejm. The Purpose of This Book 

This book explores the significant inroads women’s rights activists have made but also acknowledges the serious impediments that remain on the path to greater equality, particularly in politics. The focus of this book is specifically on nation-level legislatures and the women who enter them. While this is a relevant research site for all regions, this work explores the region of Central and Eastern Europe (CEE). This region is important to discuss because it includes many of the factors present in the world at large, factors that are promoting but also hindering the progress of women in politics. Women in this region have made strides in politics over time, as is discussed in greater detail in subsequent chapters. This has been especially significant since the fall of socialism, but their continued progress remains fragile, given the more oppositional forces actively working to assert a more traditional agenda in this part of the world. Most of the case study countries are analyzed as a collective in the effort to generalize and make inferences across them. Three of the country cases, namely Serbia, Poland, and Moldova, are examined in greater detail as separate case studies in their own subsequent chapters. Moldova is a former republic of the Soviet Union that, over the past three decades, has oscillated between pro-Russian and pro-European orientations. Thus, the cases have commonalities but are also very diverse, potentially leading to more information and associated discussion of the paths, challenges, setbacks, and victories of women leaders across the region.

Central and Eastern Europe in the Era of Durable Populism 

The countries of Central and Eastern Europe have seen a rise in right-wing populism in the second and third decades of the twenty-first century. Gains made by more progressive forces in the region have been challenged by those questioning the direction and utility of social progress and, by association, gender equality. Gender equality has become a widely accepted and frequently used term internationally. The term is related to efforts to narrow the gap in access and outcomes for men and women around the world. It is also a goal that is far from being met in any sector of society, even in advanced democracies. UN Women defines gender equality as: “… the equal rights, responsibilities and opportunities of women, men, girls and boys. Equality does not imply sameness but that the rights of women and men will not depend on the gender they were born with.” 11  Gender equality is often directly associated with women’s equality, although it refers to men also. Indeed, much of the gender-based discrimination still present in societies is directed toward women, although this is not always the case. Other populations, for example, LGBTQ+ people, face similar kinds of discrimination. Furthermore, women are certainly not a homogenous group: they have varied interests and different issues affect them. But it is the assumption of this work that gender equality in the political realm, at least, refers to closing the gap between men and women in terms of political access, representation, and power. Politics is still dominated by men across virtually all societies, and political gender equality is a goal that seeks to remedy this. Therefore, this work acknowledges various nuances in gender and gender equality but also recognizes that women share many commonalities in terms of the discrimination they face globally. Some of these challenges could be addressed and reduced by increasing their access to and presence in political power. 

In terms of resistance to these ideals, more conservative and religious elements have banded together to thwart many of the more liberal forces

By the early 1990s, levels of women’s political participation in Central and Eastern Europe had dropped to concerningly low levels. Women made up 25% of representatives in socialist-era legislatures in the mid-1980s, but by the early 1990s, this percentage had fallen to just over 10%. 12  The main cause of this precipitous drop was an abandonment of socialist-era gender quotas, tools used to guarantee a desired percentage of women in parliaments. Although socialist-era parliaments were generally undemocratic and women possessed low levels of actual political influence, governments in the socialist world were dedicated to promoting women’s rights, albeit in a “top-down” rather than “grassroots” way. 13 

With some exceptions, women’s rights in the socialist world were generally granted by government “diktat,” or by “top-down” rather than social move -

ment pressure, given the discouragement or outright ban on civil societies in socialist countries. As a result of this, women in the CEE socialist world gained some social, political, and economic opportunities—including the right to an abortion, the right to divorce, and the right to a free and quality education—but lost their ability to organize and to lobby and pressure the state in most contexts. However, mostly due to an abrupt and oft-harsh transition to capitalism and the resulting unstable economic situations of CEE countries, by the end of the 1990s, many of these gender equality gains began to recede, including those within the realm of women’s political representation. It was not until the 2010s that women began to enter the parliaments of CEE countries in greater numbers. Currently, women make up about 29% of members of parliaments in the region, representing a significant gain from the low numbers in the 1990s.

Foundational Ideas: Political Representation 

The focus of this work is situated in CEE, but it is based on extant knowledge on political representation. Hanna Pitkin’s seminal 1967 work, The Concept of Representation , discusses representation, which she defines simply as “making present in some sense something which is nevertheless not present literally or in fact.” 19  Political representation is tied to representing the electorate in spaces where they are not physically present. Representation is a key part of democratic accountability. If there is no direct link between the will of con -

stituencies, the people at large, and their political representatives, democracy ceases to function. Political representation ensures that the perspectives of people are heard and considered within decision-making bodies that have power and influence on said everyday lives. Political representation can take many forms, but representatives must be attuned to what their constituents want and need. This is related to the identity and actions of representatives. In this respect, Pitkin depicts political representation as being made up of three main categories: descriptive, substantive, and symbolic. Pitkin also puts forth a preceding category called “formalistic representation,” or rules and regulations that precede and initiate representation. 

The focus of this work is on descriptive, substantive, and symbolic representation because these kinds of representation have been linked to the literature on political representation more directly and have been discussed within the women and politics literature more readily. These three types of representation are essential for understanding how political representation works, especially in democracies, where representation and accountability are of critical importance and are often defined by state and constitutional design per se. Definitions of these kinds of representation have been developed over time. The definitions used in this work are mostly based on Pitkin’s initial definition of them and additional amendments that have been made to the definitions in later work. This original conceptual framework, although modified and contested over time, has given scholars useful tools to work with when assessing levels of political representation,

particularly that of previously marginalized or even excluded groups, including women but also racial and ethnic groups. 

Definitions of these kinds of representation are then important to broach. Descriptive representation, or “standing for” someone, is based on identity or how closely a representative “resembles” the group he or she (or they) is representing. For example, on some level, a woman descriptively repre -

sents other women by virtue of sharing that identity (assuming they both identify as women). Descriptive representation in academic literature has been associated with numerical representation. This aspect of descriptive representation of women has increased globally because the percentage of women in legislatures and politics has increased substantially over the past 25 years. This has been achieved due to the persistent activism of national and global feminist groups along with the resulting greater acceptance of gender equality norms among elite leaders and the public. 

Secondly, substantive representation, or “acting for,” refers to a representa -

tive acting on behalf of the interests of their represented group, with whom they often share an identity. For example, a woman discussing, introducing, or even sponsoring gender-sensitive legislation or legislation that furthers women’s interests as a group would involve her substantively representing other women. Notably, substantive representation has been conceptualized as occurring in two main ways. Franceschet and Piscopo argue that this kind of representation can be thought of as happening either by “process” or “outcome.” Substantive representation by “process” might entail women or representatives of other marginalized groups within legislatures in -

troducing, discussing, and debating legislation related to women’s issues, whereas representation by “outcome” entails getting legislation passed through a legislature. “Outcome” is thus linked to women politicians and their allies assuring that gender-conscious or gender equality legislation is passed as law. Franceschet and Piscopo argue that political representation occurs in both instances, even if in the case of process representation, no gender-conscious legislation is passed. They note: “Transforming political practices and winning new policies are certainly commendable instances of substantive representation as outcome, though they are not necessary for representation itself to occur.” 20  Certainly, the efforts of women in politics to raise awareness of women’s issues, such as reproductive rights, violence against women, sexual harassment, literacy, access to education, inter alia , is

an admirable and vital step toward progress. This often precedes legislative action in the form of new or amended policies and laws. Worthy initiatives require political leaders committed to them. Often these initiatives are spearheaded by groups that have a direct connection to them and a vested interest in their adoption. 

The country case studies of this book document and analyze the pro -

cesses behind legislative action in CEE countries: the advocacy women in CEE politics engage in in legislatures to make their societies more gender equal. This book includes examples of women introducing or advocating for legislation in CEE that directly benefits or at least relates to women, thus recognizing the importance of “process.” Women-led initiatives that were passed by parliaments or congresses within CEE countries are emphasized, because these efforts are emblematic of substantive progress, although “pro -

cess” based efforts, as noted, are equally necessary in this larger picture of advocacy. While both kinds of substantive representation matter, “outcome” representation can give us a clear and more direct sense of what is being done and by whom to aid women’s causes. The fate of proposed policies can also shed light on not only how far women have come in certain legislatures in terms of influencing the policy agenda, but also what kinds of challenges they face in the process. In a key sense, substantive representation is linked to the theme of this book and the findings from this research speak back to its core message: while women in CEE have made strides, as evidenced by their many efforts to change and pass existing laws, significant impediments remain and sometimes hinder them from making sustainable and lasting policy changes and reforms. 

Lastly, symbolic representation refers to the kinds of responses repre -

sentatives produce in groups with whom they share an identity. A woman representative who inspires other women to run for political office is an example of symbolic representation in practice, as her presence in politics has elicited a commitment and motivation from other women to be politi -

cally active. This is widely known as “the role model effect”. Measuring and ascertaining symbolic representation has often proven difficult in practice, however. The sections on symbolic representation in each case study chapter focus on the public perception of women in politics, in addition to public perception of key women’s issues, such as reproductive rights. The thinking behind symbolic representation is that an increase in the presence of women in politics can not only transform perceptions of women’s capabilities and belonging within politics, but also potentially transform perceptions of other, related issues, such as government efficiency and levels of corruption. The sections on symbolic representation in the case study chapters embody this 28  WomEn’s PolitiCal REPREsEntation in CEntRal and EastERn EuRoPE 

logic but also connect symbolic representation with the transformation or changes in attitudes towards women’s issues such as abortion (Poland), but also LGBTQ+ rights (Serbia) and EU membership (Moldova), assuming that symbolic representation can also involve electorates responding to the causes women leaders champion or even symbolize in more open and positive ways. Since symbolic representation has not been readily explored in the CEE region, the sections on this kind of representation are preliminary and broad, using public surveys to gauge changes in public onion across themes. 

Political representation as initially introduced by Pitkin has been a central preoccupation of many scholars of women and politics. In general, scholars have linked increases in descriptive representation with greater levels of substantive representation, although this connection does not appear in every context studied. Women make up a much larger portion of the parliaments and congresses in the CEE region than ever before, but this increase in descriptive representation has not always led to progressive changes in policy and a transformation of public perception in key areas, as the chapters elaborate. 

Guiding Frameworks in the Field of Women and Politics 

The women and politics literature has burgeoned over the past several decades. Seminal works in the field have covered significant themes related to the increasing presence of women in politics. As the number of women in the political realm has increased, so has the scholarly attention to this theme. The literature in this field has progressed through different eras. Earlier works in this important subfield of political science focused on the descriptive or numerical aspects of women in politics. Scholars such as Mansbridge 21  and Phillips 22  asserted that including more women in politics was a matter of just and equitable representation in democratic settings but they also noted the non-linear aspects of this connection, i.e. not all women are the same. Thinkers have also argued that having more women in politics is necessary because women politicians can understand the experiences of other women in a more authentic and direct way than male politicians can. They can, in turn, represent the interests and issues of women in a more comprehensive and responsive way.

Eventually, the literature on increasing the presence of women and politics became linked to the literature on gender quotas. Gender quotas are tools that countries and political parties use to increase the number of women in political institutions, most frequently legislatures, such as parliaments and congresses. Gender quotas have been instrumental in increasing the percentage of women in parliaments across national contexts. Currently, 

over 130 countries use some kind of gender quota. 23  This number has grown substantially since the 1980s, when gender quotas existed in only a handful of countries, including many in the CEE region. The early gender quota literature initially documented different kinds of quotas and weighed their efficacy. 

The typology of quotas has expanded over time. Gender quotas come in three main forms: legislated quotas, voluntary party quotas, and reserved seats. Legislated quotas are legal quotas that are enshrined in a country’s constitution or electoral law. They often mandate a minimum percentage of women that must appear on a political party’s electoral list, such as 30% or even 40%. Voluntary party quotas are quotas that political parties adopt in their respective party statutes. Generally, these quotas also call for a minimum percentage of women to be placed on electoral lists. Voluntary party quotas are just that, voluntary or optional, and are not always used by every party in the national political system. The first voluntary party quota was used in Norway in the early 1970s. Scandinavian countries, namely Sweden, Denmark, and Norway, are pioneers in women’s political representation and the early utilization of party gender quotas. The resulting higher levels of women’s political representation in those countries are linked to their early and successful efforts to aid political gender equality. Reserved seats are quotas that generally allocate a percentage of seats in parliament to women. Sometimes, these quotas also designate several electoral districts where only women can run, especially in majoritarian systems. For decades, Rwanda, an East African country with a tragic recent past and an increasingly authoritarian government, has been the world’s leader in terms of women in politics. Most notably, it is the world’s leader in the percentage of women in parliament, and it uses reserved seats, as do many countries in the Global South. Overall, legislated quotas are the most frequently used quota and the most effective. 

The quota literature first explored why countries adopt quotas at all. This was a relevant question, given that most parliaments were (and still

Outline of Chapters 

This book has seven chapters. Chapter 1 is this introduction. Chapter 2 presents a historical overview of women in politics in the CEE region. It discusses the history of women’s political representation in CEE from the beginnings of the suffrage era through the present day. This chapter empha -

sizes the state socialist period as a defining era for women in politics in the CEE region, almost indirectly so. The system is hereby called “state socialism” because full communism, as envisioned by Karl Marx, was never attained as an end goal in any CEE state. Socialism is thus a more accurate descriptor. By granting women certain fundamental rights, like the right to vote and the right to divorce, and by encouraging women to advance themselves economically and professionally, socialist governments contributed to the social empowerment of women, although the transformative effect of this remained very limited at that time. Those socialist governments, by design, were mostly led by Politburos, or executive arms of the Communist Party. So even when women were present in socialist-era legislatures, they were not generally influential in deciding on or enacting relevant laws and policies, as women were generally absent from Politburos. 

The history of women in politics in this region is also tied to the history of gender quotas, which at the time promoted women’s inclusion in socialist parliaments. Many countries in CEE, including the Soviet Union itself, used socialist-era gender or women’s quotas to promote women’s political representation. Many countries had a significant portion of women in their parliaments, despite the limitations of these women’s actual legisla -

tive power. However, when CEE countries removed gender quotas upon democratization, the descriptive representation of women fell in a stunning fashion, from over 30% in some countries to under 10% in many countries after the fall of  socialism. 30  This drop is a significant part of the history of women in politics in CEE, and it is discussed at greater length in chapter 2. It provides a historical overview of this theme in the region and important contextual information that will be relevant for subsequent chapters. Ad -

ditionally, chapter 2 emphasizes the recent history in CEE, namely the rise of right-wing populism and its effects on women’s rights and women’s political representation. The chapter argues that the combination of the lingering legacies of socialism and the current political and social challenges in the region have made the road to and life within politics arduous for women in CEE.

The chapter then dives into the state of descriptive, substantive, and symbolic representation of women. Of the three countries studied in-depth, Poland has had the most direct experience with right-wing populism; its Law and Justice Party, a right-wing populist party, was in power from 2015 to 2023. This led to a rapid rise in authoritarianism and a promotion and implementation of ultra-conservative policies, which also affected the ability of women’s groups and women politicians to represent women’s issues effectively and lobby for them formally. Unfortunately, the recent era in Polish politics represents a regressive, not a progressive, time, despite the electoral victory 36  WomEn’s PolitiCal REPREsEntation in CEntRal and EastERn EuRoPE 

of more moderate forces in 2023. However, the Polish case is also an example of the power of women’s movements to reverse authoritarian policies and stall their momentum. 

Chapter 6 includes the final in-depth case study, that of the country of Moldova. Once again, historical context is provided and then a discussion of the three kinds of political representation begins. Moldova is a case where women have made strides in the political realm, particularly descriptively. However, because Moldova’s history is intertwined with the influence of Russia, women have been historically limited in terms of what they can do to further gender equality. But, in this case, many positive breakthroughs have recently occurred, under the leadership of President Maia Sandu, Moldova’s first woman president. Thus, Moldova demonstrates that progress is possible for women in CEE, when leaders whose priority is gender equality attain power. The conclusion, chapter 7, summarizes the findings of the case studies and compares these findings to derive conclusions about the CEE region itself. The findings are then situated in a global context and linked back to leading theories and concepts in the field of women and politics. Recommendations for future research are offered, and the book ends with a call to make meaningful extensions of this work, particularly within the CEE region. 

Looking Forward 

The state of women’s political representation is a worthy goal, but it is also an important part of supporting and improving democracy. Including women’s perspectives and, of course, the perspectives of all other marginal -

ized groups, is a core part of democratic ideals and justice, not to mention a significant component of a functioning and accountable democracy. With the rise of anti-democratic sentiments in the world, it is crucial to explore the level of women’s political representation to ensure attention is paid to this theme and it is recognized as a valid and constituent part of accountable politics. Right-wing populism opposes many aspects of more progressive gender equality initiatives and is an ongoing threat to women’s political advancement. Its rise is particularly pronounced in CEE, and it remains a problem for more moderate voices in the region. Exploring the intersection of these timely themes remains significant. Through a discussion of the region’s past and present in terms of women in politics, this work discusses developments related to three main types of political representation a first put forth by Pitkin. It is argued that although women 37 intRoduC tion 

have made significant strides in the CEE region over time, their continued progress has not been straightforward or unopposed, despite their many laudable and often effective efforts. The future of equality also remains unguaranteed, especially given the uncertain reality women in politics face. The promise of progress remains present, but stubborn realities—rooted in deep, historical legacies and situated in the tumult of the contemporary political era—threaten this path to sustained progress. What follows is an in-depth discussion of the theme of women in politics in CEE and the long journey that remains to arrive at true parity, in an ever-changing era and a similarly dynamic region. 2. Divergent Paths to Suffrage: Women in Politics in CEE 

For women in the CEE region, the fight for suffrage, or the right to vote in elections (passive suffrage), and the associated right to run for office (active suffrage), overlapped temporally and substantively with the fight for suffrage in other parts of the world. The beginning of the global suffrage movement is often associated with women’s activism in Anglophone countries. The first country to grant women the right to vote and run for office was New Zealand, in 1893. 2 Activism for suffrage in the English-speaking world, in particular the United Kingdom and later the United States, defined this important era and propelled other women’s movements to fight for this foundational human right. Activists paved the way for women to organize and advocate for an expansion of rights in many CEE countries, where women’s organizations came into existence in the second half of the nineteenth century, coinciding with the rise of women’s suffrage activism in the Western world. 3

In contrast, when women gained the right to vote in the Soviet Union in 1918, it was not solely the result of grassroots women’s activism, but mostly because of the tenets of socialism. Socialism was implemented in Russia after the 1917 Revolution, which overthrew a monarchy, that of the Russian Tsar Nikolai II, by assassinating him and members of his immediate family. This revolution came to be known as the Bolshevik Revolution. The Bolshevik Revolution’s leader, Vladimir Lenin, and other contemporary socialists in the Soviet Union, primarily believed in the economic potential and value of women. Their vision for a socialist state and an ultimately socialist world included the progress of women, mostly because women were viewed as equal and crucial members of the proletariat, or the working class. Socialists believed economic empowerment would aid women’s emancipation and the promotion and growth of communism as originally envisioned by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels. As Ghodsee and Mead note: “In theory, socialism would free women from patriarchal domination by educating them and fully incorporating them into the paid labor force.” 4

Soviet women attained the right to vote two years before American women, who had advocated for decades for this right. The US suffrage

This top-down nature of socialist states affected how politics were practiced and the effect of votes in practice. Both voting and the right to run for office were constrained in most socialist systems, as embodied by Soviet Union itself. Socialist governments were not democratic, as they did not emphasize democratic elections as key to their existence and success; the representatives within those systems were not generally freely elected, despite the presence of candidates and elections. Thus, when people voted, they had very little choice for whom to vote. Women’s Political Representation During the Era of Limited Suffrage 

Once women attained the right to vote and the associated right to run for office, they were formally able to participate in politics, at least to an extent. However, the early era of women’s political involvement did not yield many women in pre-socialist legislatures, as one could expect at that time. For the most part, women’s political representation in the inter-war period remained very low. Women’s political representation in any legislature never exceeded 7% during that era. 11  It is notable that women were present at all, however, given the political and societal constraints of the time. While there were some women in these early legislatures, generally there were too few for meaningful solidarity. Their ability to effect change was also limited, given, among other impediments, the unsteady environments of their countries at the time, in the turbulent inter-war period of European history. The opportunities for any politician to effect change in these nascent democratic legislatures were limited by the lack of time and continuity. By the late 1930s, many of these legislatures had been dissolved because of the beginning of WWII and resulting foreign, in many cases Nazi German, occupations. By 1939, the chaos of war commenced on the European continent. In the devastating aftermath of WWII and in some cases years after, CEE countries adopted a socialist government, and their system of political representation dramatically changed. The reality for women in CEE also shifted, ushering in an era where women made some progress, albeit in a context of significant political and societal constraints. 

Women’s Political Representation in CEE During State Socialism 

The Larger Context 

By the end of WWII, many states within CEE adopted a state socialist system. These systems were formed in the wake of the gruesomeness and vast destruction of WWII. In some CEE countries, including Yugoslavia, socialist movements were driven by grassroots “indigenous” efforts. Many pro-socialist or pro-democratic movements in the region fought against fascist occupation during WWII. The partisan resistance of Yugoslavia, for example, fought on two ideological fronts: against the fascist occupy -

ing forces in several parts of the country and against the nationalist or

monarchist forces also vying for power, such as the “Chetniks” of  Serbia. 12 

The reality for CEE countries post-WWII mirrored the reality of much of Europe at that time. WWII devastated the entire continent, claiming millions of lives and destroying vast infrastructure, while reshaping the priorities of past and new leaders and dramatically changing the political realities of its citizens. 

Notably, Europe became separated by a symbolic but powerful divide, famously coined the “Iron Curtain” and represented by the Berlin Wall, which demarcated East Germany from the West. The eastern part of the continent fell under the sphere of influence of the Soviet Union. For the most part, Western Europe retained a capitalist and, in some cases, corresponding democratic system (other countries had totalitarian or fascist governments, such as Francisco Franco’s fascist regime in Spain, the effects of which lasted well into the 1980s). Socialist governments in CEE were generally collective in nature; they banned or severely limited private property, employed government-controlled economies, and discouraged private enterprise and free market determination of supply and demand, thereby determining the price of goods and services. Politically, in most countries, the socialist-era Politburo, determined policy. Parliaments existed but generally “rubber-stamped” the directives of the government. The media was censored and state media was central to spreading news. Education was generally free at all levels, however, and housing was often granted by the government, which developed and owned most property. Robust social welfare programs existed, such as childcare, healthcare, and pensions. Political dissent was tolerated at times and punished in other eras, also varying by  country. 13 

Within the state socialist region of Europe, women also faced a new and complex reality. In many CEE countries during the era of state socialism, women were granted more substantial rights. For example, women in several CEE countries had reproductive rights, such as the right to an abortion. Additionally, women were encouraged to attain higher levels of education, including at the secondary and tertiary levels, and education was mostly free and accessible for all people. Socialist governments also granted longer maternity leaves and sometimes free childcare and child stipends. Women were also encouraged to pursue politics, as quotas were implemented in various countries across CEE, including the Soviet Union itself. In general, women’s roles in society expanded from the mostly private to the newly

While the socialist state offered some basis for women to enter public life, its priorities were not in line with more advanced feminist goals. The state’s emphasis on workers’ rights rather than gender equality itself, coupled with the state’s non-democratic organization, limited the space for women’s political representation and activism within politics and beyond. The general intolerance of dissent and grassroots efforts also curbed the efforts of women to advocate for their causes. Therefore, while women attained greater equality, broadly conceived, during socialism, the state system was not conducive to ensuring more far-reaching and sustainable progress.

Gender Quotas and Women in Politics During Socialism 

Gender quotas were used in the state socialist system before they were used in many parts of the Western world. Voluntary party quotas were first used in Norway in the early 1970s, whereas quotas in the socialist world appeared earlier, such as in the 1930s in the Soviet Union. Some of these quotas took the form of informal quotas, as they were a part of the policy approach of many of these socialist states. The Soviet Union used formal gender quotas to bolster the number of women in their “soviets” or local  legislatures. 18 

Other countries, such as Yugoslavia, never used formal gender quotas but instead promoted women in politics informally, especially after the new constitution of 1974. 19  Despite this diversity in adoption and implementation, all CEE state socialist countries promoted greater inclusion of women in politics, despite the structural constraints that otherwise existed in the socialist system. Most countries therefore used gender quotas to include more women in politics. Socialist countries also used quotas in different areas of labor and life, but rarely did these efforts produce serious gender equality reform or even touch the epicenters of governmental power. 

As Dahlerup and Antić Gaber (2017) write: 

The fact is that under communism/socialism there were many different quota systems at work in various countries, and that quotas were installed not just for women, but also for workers, youth and other groups. At the same time, there were no quota provisions for the highest male-dominated decision-making bodies, which in many cases only had one token woman. Several studies also show that the share of women in important political bodies was not sufficiently high at any of the various levels of political decision making. The situation even worsened after the fall of the socialist/communist regimes, and women almost disappeared 

entirely from politics. 20

CEE Transitions to Democracy and Women’s Political Representation 

Gender quotas were a casualty of democratic transitions in CEE during the 1990s. When elections became competitive and free in the region, new democratic governments abandoned existing quotas, viewing them as relics of the old state system and incompatible with democratic elections and the perceived and associated values of a democratic meritocracy and “pure” competition. Gender equality initiatives in general were not prioritized at the time. What became paramount was the transition to democracy and capitalism, and in diverse countries across CEE this transition was far from smooth or ultimately equitable. At this critical point, male politicians also

Instead of building upon the gender equality efforts (as limited as they were in some cases) of previous socialist governments, transition governments emphasized other aspects, most significantly the transition of the socialist economy to a capitalist one. This proved to be an abrupt and, in some cases, disorienting transition, where many people’s living standard

Across Decades: The Waxing and Waning of Women’s Political Representation in CEE 

The story of women’s political representation in CEE is one of full of nadirs and zeniths, with many factors associated with these sometimes stark and lingering changes. Since achieving a very high percentage of women in socialist legislatures pre-transitions to democracy, CEE countries took a long time to recommit themselves to the cause of political gender equality. This is reflected in the state of numerical representation of women in parliaments across three decades, represented in the figure below.

Women were well-represented in socialist legislatures, but this level of representation dropped significantly upon transitions to democracy in the region. The level of political representation for women began to increase again steadily in the mid-2000s to now. While this recommitment to gender equality and resulting numerical increase of women in parliament are promising signs for the future, this development has not guaranteed an improvement in other kinds of representation, including substantive and symbolic. Additionally, the region is facing a right-wing populist backlash, 58  WomEn’s PolitiCal REPREsEntation in CEntRal and EastERn EuRoPE 

whose ideology and aims often target gender equality initiatives. While gender quotas themselves have not been directly rescinded in any CEE country, right-wing populist forces have attacked other aspects of gender equality programs. Examples of this abound in the region. More notably, during his time in power, the long-serving Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and his political party, Fidesz, targeted gender studies programs and have curtailed the activism of LGBTQ+ advocacy groups and other NGOs. Similarly, during its time in power in Poland, the Law and Justice Party (PiS) also curtailed women’s rights, most notably the right to an abortion. 

Despite numerical gains, women’s political representation in the region stands in a precarious place, mostly because of current geopolitical factors but also historical legacies. The hegemonic influence of an autocratic and increasingly isolated Russia is part of this current reality. Russia, like other authoritarian regimes, exports its own worldview to the regional and global stage, and this view of the world differs markedly from the previous one held during state socialism, despite both having ambitions beyond the state itself. This new approach is rooted in a primarily masculinist, expansionary, and ultimately regressive approach, one that lionizes force and historical and mythical glory. Many CEE countries, given that they exist within this realm of influence, are therefore dealing with significant external pressures and in some cases are forced to take difficult positions about their allegiances and ultimately their political priorities. 

Concurrently, there are more positive influences for the cause of gender equality. Most importantly, the counterinfluence of the European Union (EU) has been mostly constructive for many candidate countries (e.g., Serbia, Albania, Montenegro, North Macedonia, and Moldova) as they work to reform significant aspects of their laws and policies to align with EU law— the acquis communautaire . The norms the EU has “diffused” to candidate countries has encouraged them to strengthen their commitment to gender equality and, by extension, this has encouraged candidate countries to collaborate with the EU on crucial regional and global issues. Even the conversations and efforts related to gender quota adoption were influenced by EU norms and standards. Many groups vying for these reforms pointed to the spirit of the EU and its own values to convince lawmakers to adopt gender quotas. Furthermore, the quota adoption process in many countries involved persistent efforts and a substantial amount of organizing and social movement pressure, most often from women’s groups themselves. 

However, several countries in the region do not have gender quotas in any form, so there is no guarantee that the gains in women’s political representation will be sustained over time. In some countries, gender quotas 59 thE Past as PREsEnt? 

have been rejected by legislatures and even the public, partly due to the association of quotas with the “Soviet” or, more accurately, the imposing aspects of the state socialist past. Unfortunately, quotas have long been associated with a diminishment of meritocracy in politics, but in the political arenas of most countries in the world, the best candidates cannot always run in elections, let alone win, often due to the legacy of corruption, stifling of dissent, and other associated legacies of entrenched power. Therefore, pure meritocracies do not always exist in this realm. Given the currently pervasive and historically omnipresent levels of gender discrimination worldwide, quotas are one solution for reducing the inequality of women in political realms, as has been demonstrated by the progress in CEE. Quotas have helped this cause even in the CEE context, regardless of the otherwise challenging environment for gender equality efforts. But even for quotas, resistance in the region is sometimes pronounced and cannot always be countered by appeals to higher authorities, such as the European Union. The EU can recommend the promotion of gender equality and even mandate some of it directly through the acquis, but it cannot and does not require candidate countries to adopt gender quotas. The adoption of quotas is therefore a mostly domestic concern and requires domestic activism and broader public and elite-level support. 

CEE History as Foundational and Its Effects as Ongoing 

This historical chapter on CEE women in politics has discussed several eras of this umbrella theme. The chapter first explored the suffrage era in the region and its effects on women’s political representation. While there were many suffrage activists across CEE countries that helped secure the right to vote for women, even before WWII, much of their legacy was lost in the subsequent historical developments of the region. While the state socialist systems that arose after WWII employed their own versions of political gender equality, these systems were run mostly from the top down, and gender equality grassroots activism became obsolete, mostly because this kind of activism was forbidden or discouraged by new socialist governments. Even though women’s political representation increased in this system numerically, the effects of this were mostly “cosmetic” as virtually no legislator in this system could introduce or even advocate for meaningful reforms. Decisions were generally made in socialist Politburos and not in respective national parliaments. 60  WomEn’s PolitiCal REPREsEntation in CEntRal and EastERn EuRoPE 

However, government initiatives in the socialist era helped women to an extent. Gender quotas enabled many women to enter socialist-era parliaments, thus enabling a generation of women to participate in this otherwise masculine realm. But upon the transition to democracy in the early 1990s, socialist-era gender quotas were abandoned by all CEE states. It would take two decades for countries to truly re-embrace gender quotas and reattain previous levels of women’s political representation. As this chapter notes, it was this effort to readopt gender quotas that eventually increased the percentage of women in CEE parliaments to the current level of close to 30%, which is above the world average. This chapter also provided historical context related to the broader theme of women in politics in CEE by discussing several eras that influenced the women in contemporary politics. While women were viewed as equals in the proletarian struggle during socialism, they were still expected to act according to traditional norms in the private sphere. Socialism did not do enough to change attitudes in this private realm. This lack of progress is also reinforced in the reality women face today, with heightened backlash stemming from right-wing populist narratives that emphasize women’s roles as mostly belonging to the private sphere. This chapter argues that women’s political representation in CEE was defined by unique but also universal circumstances. Like many women in the world, CEE women used the opportunities available to them to further their gender equality goals. Without their efforts, the region would not be even as equal as it is today. 

While this chapter focused on the historical dimensions of the broader theme, the subsequent chapter will explore relevant concepts of political representation. Previous research and writing on political representation will first be explored, and then the application of this relevant work to the women and politics research will be discussed. This will be followed by a review of relevant literature related to each type of political representation and a discussion of each type of representation globally and in the CEE region. 3.  The Importance of Political Representation: The Origins, Applications, and Varied Implications of a Central Concept 

Abstract: Chapter 3 introduces the conceptual framework the book uses, namely Pitkin’s types of political representation. First, it briefly discusses the historical thinking related to political representation, eventually connecting this to the seminal Pitkin work. The chapter ties her work to its profound influences on the literature on women’s political representation. Then the chapter turns to a more in-depth exploration of each type of representation, noting relevant literature within each representation category. Themes across notable works are noted, as is the overall state of women’s political representation within each category, both regionally and globally. The chapter concludes by linking democratic progress to women’s political representation in CEE and beyond.

The concept of political representation has preoccupied political philoso -

phers and scholars for a very long time, in both direct and indirect ways. Although ancient Greek texts did not deal directly with the concept of representation (as the actual practice of it was limited in that era), the work of philosophers at that time remains relevant for discussions of democracy and by extension, representation of the demos , or the people. Aristotle’s thinking on the polity and what it means to be a good citizen and live the “good life” set a foundation for more contemporary discussions of

the responsibility of political representatives in our modern era. Indeed, the concept of representation is key to understanding democracy and to improving it in theory and practice. After all, political representatives are supposed to “represent,” and, by extension, “stand for” their constituents. They also are, or at least should be, held accountable for their choices and actions. What this means and how it works vary greatly across temporal, political, and national contexts. 

Scholars, including Hanna Pitkin herself, trace more modern interpreta -

tions of political representation to the work of English philosopher Thomas Hobbes, who wrote his seminal works in the seventeenth century and whose treatise The Leviathan is one of the most influential texts in the field of classical political science. The Leviathan is a work that discusses basic social organization, and it maintains that a social contract is necessary between people and governments to enforce necessary order and diminish natural chaos. Absolute freedom is exchanged between a government and its citizens for a set of laws and rules that make existence more stable and ultimately endurable. Life in the “state of nature” is too “nasty, brutish and short” to facilitate meaningful existence, therefore a strong “sovereign” is needed to enforce laws. 1 Hobbes’s work argues that humans need to overcome their “primitive” states of nature, and this tenet remains foundational for much of political philosophy, even influencing the field of international relations, whose scholars use Hobbes’s concept of a “state of nature” to describe the international realm, where an “anarchy,” or absence of a central government, exists to this day. 2

However, Hobbes’s original work has limitations for the concept of political representation in our modern era. His idea of representation as needing to be “absolute” because a populace generally authorizes a repre -

sentative to represent them absolutely is problematic because it proposes an anti-democratic view of representing citizens. Pitkin, in response to Hobbes, calls for a different kind of political representation that authorizes a representative to “stand for” and “act for” a group, but not in absolute terms and not without due consideration of the group’s priorities and interests. Indeed, political representation, to Pitkin and in more ideal terms, should involve more deliberate and collaborative or at least cooperative aspects.

A representative should act independently but not without reflection on his or her constituency’s best interests. 

Political representation, just like democracy itself, has, as a concept, been expanded over time. Hobbes’s view of political representation was just the start. Political philosophers and scholars of the field have refined this concept over time to make it more applicable to and useful for the contemporary era. Most relevantly for this work, Pitkin reinforces this idea of what representation is and contributes other core concepts to this theme. She introduces four main types of representation in practice—formalistic, descriptive, substantive, and symbolic representation—and delineates what they are and how they they function. Formalistic representation partly refers to the rules of elections, how representatives are chosen. Electoral laws and procedures vary across national contexts. Surely, the way elections are organized is crucial for political representation. For example, having a parliamentary system with proportional representation rather than a majoritarian system affects the way people are represented in a country. In the US, the absence of a third party marginalizes people who do not identify with either major party, leaving them with fewer options at the voting booth. European democracies, on the other hand, often have smaller political parties in their parliaments that represent unique, nuanced, and often avant-garde viewpoints of the populace. Parliamentary systems therefore generally offer more options to voters, even though power also resides within larger and longer-standing, mainstream parties. Rules and procedures are thus important aspects of representation to document and examine. 

However, Pitkin’s work offers other more useful terms and concepts that have been discussed by scholars much more directly and thoroughly. Indeed, the remaining three types of representation have been given much more attention, especially in the literature about women and politics. Descriptive representation, which refers to how well a representative “resembles” their constituents in terms of identity markers (e.g., gender, race, class), has greatly influenced the literature on the representation of women. The idea is that the more closely a representative resembles his or her constituency according to identity characteristics, the better the representative can represent his or her constituents. Pitkin called this “standing for” a group. This concept has been used by women and politics scholars to argue for an increase in women’s political representation. 3 Presumably, women representatives identify with women constituents more strongly than men and therefore can represent

them in a more informed and responsive manner. The concept of descriptive representation is linked to subsequent “substantive representation,” or what Pitkin linked to “acting for.” In this type of representation, representatives who share a common identity with a group are expected to advocate for said group through the promotion of certain values and beliefs and associated policies that could further that group’s interests and improve their quality of life. Women and politics scholars have also used this proposed connection in their research. It is thought that women, especially once they attain a significant presence in legislatures, begin to advocate for women’s interests and issues. But this assertion remains contested in the literature, and in practice it is not always so linear. 4

There is also the concept of symbolic representation, which refers to the ability of representatives to act as transformative symbols for groups they represent. Namely, the presence of certain representatives in a political body can evoke feelings among voters or constituents, and can potentially change perceptions and attitudes, and even inspire different thinking or action among those represented. Examples of this would be an increase in women in parliament changing the public’s perception of women as politicians or the parliament itself, as to view them more favorably. Another example is the increase of women in a political body inspiring more women to vie for positions within this institution, again called “the role model effect”. Women and politics scholars have also used this concept to evaluate the effects of increased descriptive representation of women on perceptions of women in politics. These studies have generally shown a positive association between the two types of representation that emphasize “standing for” in different ways. Descriptive representation and symbolic representation are therefore linked; while descriptive representation emphasizes shared identity as being a conduit for better representation within institutions, symbolic representation emphasizes shared identity as being a part of a change in public perception and eventually broader societal change. 

This work recognizes all three types of political representation as being important, but it argues that descriptive representation, or increasing the presence of marginalized groups, is often a necessary, but perhaps insuf -

ficient, precursor for the rest. Substantive representation, while significant, is generally facilitated by the increased presence of previously excluded groups in political institutions. While actors who do not share the same identity characteristics as a group can and do represent their interests in a political
